# ARISTOTLE'S ETHICS
## THE GREATER NICOMACHEAN [ETHICS] BOOK <unclear>1</unclear> <note>The title "Greater Nicomachean" is a hybrid; the text is actually the "Magna Moralia" or "Great Ethics."</note>

</margin>
Since we propose to speak about character, we must first consider what branch of knowledge character is a part of. To put it briefly, it seems to be a part of nothing other than <term>politics</term> <note>original: "πολιτικῆς" (politikēs); for Aristotle, politics is the "master science" of how humans live together well.</note>. For in political affairs, it is not possible to act at all without being a person of a certain quality—and by this I mean, for example, being <term>virtuous</term> <note>original: "σπουδαῖον" (spoudaion); literally "serious" or "excellent," referring to a person of high moral standing.</note>. To be virtuous is to possess the virtues. Therefore, if anyone intends to be effective in political matters, they must be of a good character. Thus, character seems to be both a part and the starting point of politics. <gloss>of ethics</gloss> This study of character, as a branch of politics, <gloss>ethical</gloss> <gloss>the name of character</gloss> seems to me to be rightly named "Ethics." <margin>of ethics</margin> For both politics and ethics deal with character. <gloss>ethics</gloss> It is necessary, therefore, as it seems, to first speak about <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "ἀρετῆς" (aretēs); better understood as "excellence" or "functional perfection."</note>—what it is and from what it arises. For there is no benefit in knowing what virtue is, if one does not also know how...

...of the father’s nature; therefore it was not likely for him to truly enjoy <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "ἀρετῆς" (aretēs); meaning excellence or moral virtue.</note>. By not taking the error of dividing the soul into its parts—specifically those having reason—correctly, he failed; and yet he assigned to each its fitting virtues. Thus far, he did well. After this, however, he was no longer correct. For he mixed his treatment of virtue with the study of the "excess of the good" <note>This refers to Plato's "Form of the Good," which the author argues is too abstract for a practical study of ethics.</note>. I do not dare say this to the philosopher <note>referring to Plato</note>. For if this were the case, perhaps he should have only spoken if he had not examined those things later.

Therefore, if for all powers the end is a good <gloss>regarding the whole body and every power</gloss>, it is clear that the end of the best power would be the best good. For concerning the good of the gods, there is another discourse, and no equal investigation; but concerning the political good, we must speak of the good for us.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous discussion regarding the "Idea of the Good" toward a more practical investigation of virtue. While the previous page critiqued abstract forms, this page focuses on the distinction between theoretical knowledge (science) and moral character (virtue), and begins a systematic classification of different types of "goods."</meta>

Why is it that, in the case of the sciences, it <gloss>sometimes</gloss> happens that one simultaneously knows <gloss>both</gloss> the science and is a scientist? For instance, if someone <unclear>knows</unclear> medicine, <unclear>this person</unclear> is also a physician. It is the same in the case of the other sciences. But this does not happen in the case of the virtues. For if someone knows what justice is, he is not immediately a just man; the same applies to the other virtues. Is it possible then that the virtues are, and at the same time are not, sciences? Since these matters have been distinguished,

<margin>What is the division of the goods?</margin>
let us attempt to say how many categories the **goods** <note>original: "ἀγαθὰ" (agatha); things that are beneficial or desirable.</note> occupy. Of these goods,
<margin>What are the honored goods?</margin>
some are **honored**, others are **praiseworthy**, and others are **potential**. By the "honored," I mean something such as the divine and the best—for example, the **soul** <note>original: "ψυχή" (psyche); the vital principle or seat of character.</note> and the **mind** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous); intellect or intuitive reason.</note>. Also included are the most ancient things, the first principle, and such things. Honored things are those <gloss>to which</gloss> honor is given. Indeed, honor follows all such things. Virtue is not an honored good,
<margin>What are the praiseworthy goods?</margin>
because <gloss>from</gloss> virtue one becomes an excellent person. Now, wealth <gloss>is</gloss> a form of virtue that has come to be; but the **praiseworthy** goods are, for example, the <term>virtues</term> <note>original: "ἀρεταί" (aretai); qualities of excellence. In this context, they are "praiseworthy" because they require effort and action.</note>. For praise arises from the <unclear>actions</unclear> <gloss>for</gloss> performed according to them.
<margin>What are the potential goods?</margin>
Then there are the **potential** goods, such as power, wealth, strength, and beauty. For these are things that the excellent man could use well, and the base man could use badly. Therefore, such things are called "potential" goods. They are indeed goods, but their status is proven by the use of the excellent man.

<summary>This page distinguishes between theoretical knowledge and moral virtue, noting that knowing what justice is does not make one just. It further categorizes "the good" into honored things (the soul), praiseworthy things (the virtues), and potential goods (wealth and power).</summary>

<keywords>virtue, knowledge, justice, classification of goods, soul, mind, wealth, potentiality, praise, excellence</keywords>

An **incomplete** good is that which, when it is present, we require something more. For example, when justice is present, we still require many <gloss>other</gloss> things. But when **happiness** <note>original: "εὐδαιμονία" (eudaimonia); often translated as "flourishing," this refers to the highest state of human well-being.</note> is present, we no longer require anything. This, then, is the "best" for us which we seek, which is the **end** <note>original: "τέλος" (telos); the ultimate goal or final purpose of an action.</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from discussing the "nutritive" soul—the basic biological functions of life—to a higher division of human psychology. It begins to categorize specific virtues (like wisdom and courage) based on whether they belong to the rational or irrational parts of the soul, setting the stage for the famous "doctrine of the mean."</meta>

<margin>
**Division**
**of the soul:**
the parts of the rational
part of the soul;
</margin>
Having spoken of these matters in another way, let us now define them: <gloss>concerning virtue</gloss> **first, then, let us speak** about the soul in which <gloss>virtue</gloss> resides. It is not so much a question of what the soul *is*—which is a subject for a much longer discussion—but rather how it is commonly described. We say the soul is divided into two parts: the rational <note>original: logon echon, literally "having reason"</note> and the irrational <note>original: alogon</note>. Within the rational part, there arise practical wisdom <term>phronēsis: the ability to discern the right course of action in specific situations</term>, quickness of mind, wisdom, ease of learning, memory, and similar qualities. In the irrational part, however, we find what are called the virtues: for example, temperance <term>sōphrosunē: self-control, particularly regarding physical pleasures</term>, justice, and courage. These are the qualities of character <note>original: ēthous</note> that are considered praiseworthy. Indeed, it is because of these that we are called "praiseworthy." Yet, regarding the excellences of the rational part, no one is praised in quite the same way. One is not "praised" simply for being wise or for having practical wisdom <note>In Greek thought, moral praise is reserved for choices and character, while intellectual skill is admired or congratulated but not "praised" as a moral achievement.</note>; in short, no one is praised for these sorts of intellectual things. Nor <margin>Note</margin> indeed which of these is foundational, though the irrational part serves the rational part.

---

<margin>**moral virtue.**</margin>
**Since moral virtue** is destroyed by deficiency and excess, we must recognize that both deficiency and excess lead to ruin. This can be clearly seen through things perceptible to our senses. We must use visible evidence to testify to things that are hidden <note>This is a core Aristotelian method: using physical, observable analogies (like health) to explain invisible, ethical concepts.</note>. One can see this immediately in the case of **physical exercise**: if it is done in excess, strength is destroyed, and likewise if there is too little. The same is true of **food and drink**: if too much is consumed, it destroys one's health, just as too little does.

<summary>This page divides the human soul into rational and irrational parts to distinguish between intellectual skills and moral virtues. It introduces the principle that moral virtue, like physical health, is a balance that is destroyed by the extremes of excess or deficiency.</summary>

Regarding desire <term>desire: *orexis* — the general capacity for reaching out toward an object, encompassing both rational and irrational impulses</term>, there are <gloss>three</gloss> types: appetite, spirit, and wish. is accompanied by reason <note>original: *logos*</note>. And reason belongs to none of the irrational animals. Desire, on the one hand, comes from impulse—for I say it is without deliberation. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, specifically focusing on Book III, Chapter 3. But in the sciences, this is not the case. No one <gloss>at all</gloss> deliberates about how one ought to write the name "Archicleous" <note>original: "Ἀρχικλεούς". **Modesty** <term>Modesty: "aidos," a sense of shame or a moral "blushing" that prevents one from doing disgraceful things.</term> is a mean between shamelessness and bashfulness. ## **Friendliness**
**Friendliness** <term>Friendliness: "philia," referring here to the social virtue of being pleasant in company, rather than deep personal affection.</term> is a mean <note>the middle ground or "virtuous balance"</note> between flattery and hostility. It is concerned with actions in words. On one hand, the flatterer <note>original: "kolax"</note> is the one who adds more than is fitting and pretends to give more than he has. On the other hand, the quarrelsome person <note>original: "apekhthaltikos," one who is prone to hatred or conflict</note> is an enemy, taking away from even the things that already exist. But the other person, who is as he ought to be, is the mean. The friend <note>The text uses "friend" here to describe the person possessing the virtue of friendliness.</note> is not able to be equal in this way: for he will not add present things which do not exist, nor will he treat things that are not fitting as if they were fitting; nor will he make things that are not more seem less, nor will he falsely oppose what seems right to him. Thus, the friend is such a person.

But the truthful person will do neither of these; for he will neither pretend to have more than he has, nor less. Instead, he will say that the things he has, he indeed has, and what he knows, he knows. Is the truthful person, then, a virtue or not a virtue? He will say, the truthful person...

<meta>This page continues the transition from general ethics to the specific study of Justice. Having established that justice is a "complete virtue" in the previous section, the author now begins to analyze the mathematical and proportional nature of justice, specifically defining it as a "mean" or middle state between extremes of gain and loss.</meta>

<margin>
Much
Excess
Just. Middle.
Deficiency
Little
</margin>

Simply speaking, the just is that which relates to another as equality. The unjust, conversely, is the unequal. When more of the good things are assigned to oneself, and less of the evils, this is unequal and not just; it is, in fact, injustice. For it is clear that injustice exists in unequal distributions, while justice itself is a kind of middle state <term>middle state: "mesotes," the virtuous balance between two extremes</term> between excess and deficiency, and between "much" and "little." For the one who acts unjustly gains more than their share <note>original: "pleonektei," meaning to overreach or take more than one's fair portion</note>. And the one who is treated unjustly receives less. This middle point is the "just." The middle is equality. Thus, one may say that the equal point between "more" and "less" is the just.

The just person, then, is the one who wishes to have what is equal. For equality in proportional matters is [sometimes] deficient <note>The author is likely referencing the distinction between simple arithmetic equality (everyone gets the same) and proportional equality (rewards based on merit or contribution)</note>. For to be equal toward another is just, and the person who acts this way is just in themselves. <insert>S</insert>ince, then, justice resides in what is just and consists of a middle state, in what things does the "just" exist? The "just" is equal—it is equal to something—and the "middle" is a middle between certain things. Therefore, justice and the "just" will exist in relation to certain people and within certain circumstances. 

It will be clear, then, that the just is equal, and justice is this very thing: an equality of amount. Proportion <note>original: "analogon"</note> exists in both the greatest and the smallest things. Just as it is fitting to have what is proper, it is proportional for those who possess many things to contribute much, and for those who possess little to contribute little. Similarly for everyone, the one who has labored much...

<summary>This page defines justice as a mathematical 'mean' or middle state of equality between the extremes of having too much (excess) and having too little (deficiency). It introduces the concept of proportional justice, where contributions and rewards are balanced according to a person's status or effort.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of justice as a form of proportion, moving from the theoretical definition of the "middle state" to the practical application of distributive and reciprocal justice within a community. ...to receive much. And the one who has done little, to receive little. As the one who has acted relates to the one who has not, so do the "many things" relate to the "few things." As the one who has done much relates to much, so the one who has not [done much] relates to little. 

The use of the just, according to proportion <term>proportion: "analogia," the mathematical relationship between different values or people</term>, exists within the city. For instance, they say the farmer produces grain; the builder, a house; the weaver, a garment; and the shoemaker, a sandal. The farmer gives grain to the builder, and the builder gives a house to the farmer. Similarly with the other crafts, they are so arranged that what is produced by them is exchanged for the remaining things in turn. 

This is indeed proportion: as the farmer is to the builder, so is the builder to the farmer. Likewise for the shoemaker, the weaver, and all the others.

<margin>8</margin> The same proportion applies to everyone. And this same proportion belongs to each by virtue of the city-state <note>original: "poleia," likely referring to the civic community or political structure</note>. So that the just is the reciprocal <term>reciprocal: "antapodon," the act of giving back in return or "tit-for-tat" exchange</term>. 

And it is this justice that holds cities together. Justice is the same as reciprocity. However, since the builder's work is of greater value than the shoemaker's—or indeed his many works—and since this craft is valued differently for the shoemaker compared to the builder, it was not possible to simply receive a house in exchange for a sandal. At this point, money <term>money: "nomisma," derived from the word for "law" or "custom," representing a social convention used to measure value</term> was introduced as the means for <unclear>carrying out transactions</unclear>.

### Definition of the Involuntary.

<margin>
Regarding
ignorance
</margin>

Regarding ignorance, we must also provide a definition: how ignorance arises so that an act is not <unclear>harmful</unclear> or considered the commission of injustice. The definition is as follows: whenever ignorance is the cause <insert>or</insert> of the performance of an act, one does not do it voluntarily. Consequently, one does not commit an injustice <note>In Greek ethics, an "injustice" (adikēma) requires the intent or "will" of the actor; without it, the act may be harmful but not morally "unjust" in the same way</note>. However, when the person is themselves the cause of their ignorance and acts according to <gloss>a certain</gloss> ignorance, the cause resides within them; they nonetheless commit an injustice, and such a person will be called the cause <note>literally "justly called the cause"</note> of the act. 

<margin>Just as</margin> for example, in the case of those who are drunk: for those who are drunk and perform some evil deed commit an injustice. They themselves are the causes of their ignorance, for it was in their power not to drink to such an extent that, through ignorance, they might strike their own father. 

Similarly, regarding other types of ignorance: in all cases where the ignorance occurs through the people themselves, those committing injustice are indeed doing wrong. But in cases where they are not the causes of the ignorance themselves, but rather the circumstances of the actions are the cause, they do not commit injustice. Such ignorance is "natural" ignorance. 

For instance, children act in ignorance of what they are doing. In these cases, because the ignorance is natural, it does not mean they act voluntarily in those things where children are said to "do wrong" <note>Aristotle often distinguishes between a "wrong act" (doing something harmful) and "committing injustice" (acting with a settled character and intent)</note>. The ignorance is the cause of the performance of these acts, but they are not the cause of the ignorance; therefore, they are not said to commit an injustice.

In the same way, the virtues also become praiseworthy. From this it follows that **natural virtue** <term>original: *physikē aretē*; an innate disposition toward good behavior that exists before it is refined by education or reason.</term> by itself exists without reason. When it is separated from reason, it is of little value and is not praiseworthy. Yet virtue must be something praiseworthy. But when it is joined to **right reason** <term>original: *orthos logos*; the rational principle that guides correct action.</term> and **deliberate choice** <term>original: *proairesis*</term>, it makes virtue complete. Therefore, that too is right reason. Indeed, the natural impulse toward virtue cannot exist without right reason. Nor, on the other hand, can reason and deliberate choice constitute virtue entirely without the natural impulse. 
<margin>Socrates</margin>
For this reason, **Socrates** <note>The author refers to the famous Greek philosopher's view that "virtue is knowledge," suggesting that if one knows what is right, one will inevitably do it.</note> was not correct when he claimed that the virtues are identical to reason. For he argued that it is not through **prudence** <term>original: *phronēsis*; practical wisdom.</term> that we exist and perform acts of courage or justice, but rather that we choose them by reason based on an opinion. Therefore, to say that virtue *is* reason is incorrect. He says it is better put this way: "To act in accordance with right reason is to do what is good," which is why they say virtue exists. Reason itself is correct. Yet someone might perform just actions without any deliberate choice, not even knowing what ought to be done, but acting from some irrational impulse. They might act rightly and even in accordance with right reason. For I mean that they acted exactly as right reason commanded. Nevertheless, such an action is not praiseworthy. He says it is better that we define it this way: that virtue is the impulse toward the **noble** <note>original: *to kalon*; often translated as "the beautiful" or "the fine," representing moral excellence.</note> accompanied by reason. For this is what constitutes virtue and is praiseworthy. One might wonder whether prudence itself is a virtue or not. Yet it is <unclear>manifest</unclear> <unclear>manifest</unclear> to all that it is indeed a virtue.

<summary>This page argues that true virtue requires a harmony between natural impulses and right reason, rejecting Socrates' theory that virtue is simply a form of rational knowledge. ...where there are better things, **Prudence** <term>original: *phronēsis*</term> would not seem to be their ruler. <margin>Equity and the equitable man.</margin>
<margin>2nd item to be done</margin>
Since it is necessary to make an investigation into each of these virtues, and to address their specific natures in their proper places, we must next discuss **equity** <term>original: *epieikeia*; a sense of fairness that goes beyond the literal letter of the law</term> and the **equitable man**. We must see how equity relates to **justice** <term>original: *dikaiosynē*</term> and the **just**. For to those who examine the matter, equity appears to be neither simply the same as justice, nor something entirely different in kind. 

At times we praise equity and the man who possesses it, so much so that we even use the term "equitable" as a substitute for "good" when describing other things, showing that to be more equitable is to be better. Yet, at other times, if we follow a logical argument, it seems strange if the equitable—being something separate from the just—is praiseworthy. For if they are different, either justice is not something excellent, or equity is not just. If they are both excellent, then they must be the same thing.

<meta>This page continues the transition into the specific ethical virtues within Book II of the *Magna Moralia* (Great Ethics). Following the discussion of equity—the spirit of the law versus the letter—the text now introduces "good judgment" and "good deliberation," explaining how they function alongside prudence to guide human action toward the best possible outcomes.</meta>

**Judgment** <term>original: *eugnōmosynē*; the capacity to judge fairly or with good sense</term> and the **person of good judgment** <term>original: *eugnōmōn*</term> are concerned with the same matters as **equity** <term>original: *epieikeia*; fairness that goes beyond the strict letter of the law</term>.
<margin>Good judgment and the man of good judgment.</margin>
These concern both matters of justice and those things omitted by the legislator because he did not define them with absolute precision. Judgment is the ability to evaluate what was missed by the legislator, things that could not be stated explicitly within the law. While one can be "of good judgment" regarding justice, **good judgment** does not exist without equity. For to judge is the role of good judgment, but the practical application of that judgment is the work of the equitable person.

<margin>Good deliberation</margin>
Now, **good deliberation** <term>original: *euboulia*; the quality of taking good counsel</term> is concerned with the same things as **prudence** <term>original: *phronēsis*; practical wisdom</term>. It deals with matters of action, which is also the domain where the virtues exist. However, it does not exist without prudence. For while prudence is the active implementation of these things, good deliberation is the disposition <unclear>which</unclear> is successful at attaining what is best and most advantageous in practical affairs.

For this reason, such outcomes do not stem from good deliberation if they happen spontaneously or by **chance** <term>original: *tychē*</term>. In those for whom prior <unclear>deliberation</unclear> is not guided by reason, it is not possible—to put it simply—to become a person of good counsel through this kind of mind. Successes that occur without the guidance of a judging reason are merely **good luck** <term>original: *eutychēma*</term>. For sometimes there is an attainment of justice, if it is a matter of giving what is equal to each person. He says that whatever kind of person someone is, they encounter the law in a corresponding way; for this reason, he says, one cannot even flee from punishment. —

It distinguishes these rational virtues from mere good luck, which achieves the right result without the use of reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the relationship between practical wisdom (prudence) and moral character. Having previously defined "good deliberation" as the successful pursuit of the best ends, the text now explores the specific knowledge required for justice and how it differs from the general knowledge of "goods," using the medical art as a primary analogy for ethical application.</meta>

<margin>
(red symbol)
To render
</margin>

To **render to each person according to their worth** <note>original: *to kat’ axian hekastō apodidonai*</note> would certainly seem to be the mark of both a **just** and an **excellent** man. Yet one might raise a difficulty here. Since acting unjustly consists of harming someone voluntarily, while knowing whom, to what extent, and for what purpose one does so. Indeed, harm and **injustice** <term>original: *adikia*</term> occur in relation to **goods** and concerning things that are good. For the unjust man is the one who <unclear>does not know</unclear> what kinds of things are truly good and what kinds are evil. 

<margin>
(black symbol)
</margin>

To know the circumstances of one's actions is the particular characteristic of the **prudent man** and of **prudence** <term>original: *phronēsis*; practical wisdom or moral discernment</term>. It would be absurd if the greatest good—prudence—were to accompany the unjust man. Or rather, prudence does not seem to follow the unjust man at all; for if it did, he would never be unjust. For he would not be able to judge what is **simply good** <gloss>simply good: things that are inherently beneficial for all humans in an absolute sense</gloss> and what is good for himself <gloss>specifically</gloss> without falling into error. It is the role of prudence to be able to contemplate these matters correctly. 

This is similar to what we see in the **medical art** <term>original: *iatrikē*; the science of medicine</term>. We recognize things that are simply healthy, and no less effective at producing health—all the Greeks <note>The author uses "the Greeks" here to refer to common cultural knowledge regarding medical practices.</note> know of **hellebore** <note>original: *helleboros*; a plant used in ancient medicine as a powerful, often dangerous, purgative</note>, purgatives, **surgery** <note>original: *tomai*; literally "cuttings"</note>, and **cautery** <note>original: *kauseis*; "burnings" used to seal wounds or treat infections</note>. Yet medicine is no less a science because of this. We do not yet know the specific good for each individual case in the same way doctors know that *this* treatment is good for *these* specific people and *at this specific time*. This depends on how we are physically disposed, and this is where medical science truly operates. Therefore, we do not possess these things which we call "simply healthy" in a vacuum.

<summary>This page discusses the definition of justice as rendering what is due and argues that true injustice involves a failure of prudence, as the unjust man lacks the practical wisdom to discern true goods. The author uses medical treatments like surgery and cautery to illustrate that while general "goods" are known to all, the science lies in knowing how to apply them to specific individuals.</summary>

<page-num>37</page-num>

<margin>
e
but
X
</margin>

...a knowledgeable person, while in a state of sleep, can be thought of as having a dual nature, just as **knowledge** <term>original: *epistēmē*</term> must be active within them. It is exactly the same for the person who is **lacking self-control** <term>original: *akratēs*</term>. For their knowledge is like that of a sleeper when it is not being exercised. Thus, the **puzzle** <term>original: *aporia*</term> is solved; the path of the argument helps us see why it is that those lacking self-control [act against their knowledge]. It seemed strange that knowledge could be cast aside, for it is thought to be [the most powerful thing]. We explain the matter from this point: as we stated in the **Analytics** <note>Aristotle’s works on logic, specifically the *Prior Analytics*, which discuss how conclusions are drawn from premises</note>, a **syllogism** <term>original: *syllogismos*; a logical deduction</term> arises from two premises. This is the practical application. He illustrates this through particular instances. For example: "I know that everyone with a **fever** <term>original: *pyretos*</term> [requires a specific treatment] for health..."

<margin>
<image-desc>A small downward-pointing triangle representing a logical structure (syllogism). To the right of the triangle are the words "substances" and "of fever". To the left are "horse," "the one acts," and "acts." Below the point of the triangle is the mark "of the fever".</image-desc>
</margin>

"...and this person here has a fever." <gloss>all... produces knowledge</gloss> "I know, therefore, that I must make this person healthy." <gloss>Absurd; on the one hand... or the universal knowledge</gloss> In this case, I have the **universal** <term>original: *katholou*; a general rule or category</term> knowledge, but I do not have the knowledge of the **particular** <term>original: *epi merous*; the specific, individual instance</term>. The error occurs here, even when someone possesses knowledge. For example: "everyone [knows that] a fever must be healed," but as for the person actually suffering the fever, I do not recognize it. Likewise, then, in the case of the person **lacking self-control**, this same failure of knowledge will occur. In this state, the person lacks self-control despite having the universal knowledge—for instance, the rule that "sweet things are bad and harmful." He fails to act on this because of the **particular** instance; he sees that "this thing is sweet," and because his knowledge is not being actively used, he will err. He possessed the universal [rule], but not the [recognition of] the particular. He does not work it out.

<summary>This page explains the "practical syllogism" to show how a person can know a general rule (like "fever is bad") but fail to apply it to a specific situation (like "this person has a fever"). This logical gap explains how "lack of self-control" is possible, comparing the state of the person to someone who is asleep.</summary>

<margin>Concerning self-control and endurance</margin>

One might ask whether **self-control** <term>original: *enkrateia*; the power to resist pleasure</term> and **endurance** <term>original: *karteria*; the power to withstand pain</term> are perhaps the same thing. For self-control is concerned with pleasures; the self-controlled person is the one who masters pleasures. However, endurance is concerned with pains. For the enduring person is the one who holds out against them; this is what makes him enduring.

<margin>Softness, and the soft person, and the one lacking self-control.</margin>

In relation to lack of self-control, **softness** <term>original: *malakia*; often associated with an effeminate lack of resolve</term> does not possess its <gloss>own distinct nature</gloss>. For softness exists, and the "soft" person is the one who does not endure hardships—not all hardships, but those which one is nevertheless expected to endure. By contrast, the person lacking self-control is the one who is unable to hold out against pleasures. He is both <unclear>becoming soft</unclear> and <unclear>enslaved</unclear> by this state.

<margin>The intemperate and the one lacking self-control.</margin>

There is, again, a person called **intemperate** <term>original: *akolastos*; one who is shamelessly devoted to pleasure</term>. Is the intemperate person the same as the one lacking self-control, or not? 

<margin>Distinct qualities</margin>

<margin>Goodwill.</margin> **Goodwill** <term>eunoia: a well-wishing that lacks the intensity or shared life of true friendship</term> seems to be like friendship, but it is not. Therefore, perhaps one might properly be called **self-sufficient** <gloss>self-sufficient</gloss> <term>autarkēs: someone who has everything they need within themselves and requires nothing from the outside</term>; <insert>for they used [this term]</insert>

What, then, will He contemplate? <meta>This page continues the discussion on whether a self-sufficient person needs friends. <unclear>to</unclear> contemplate, they say. Just as when we wish to see our own face, we look into a **mirror** <term>katoptron: used here as a metaphor for the social "mirror" provided by a companion</term> and see a likeness, so also if we wish to know ourselves, we might recognize ourselves by looking at a friend. And indeed, this "knowing of oneself" is not possible without a friend; for the self-sufficient man requires friendship for the purpose of knowing himself.

## ARISTOTLE'S ECONOMICS: BOOK ONE

<margin>
The subject <unclear>matter</unclear> <note>original: hypokeimenon; literally the "underlying thing" or topic.</note> of household management is the house; that of political science is the city.
</margin>

**H**ousehold management <note>original: oikonomikē; the root of our word "economics," though here it specifically means managing a domestic estate.</note> and political science differ. They differ not only as much as a house and a city—for these are their respective subjects—but it is also clear that political science consists of many rulers, while household management is a monarchy. Now, some of the arts are divided, and it does not belong to the same art to produce something and to use what has been produced, as is the case with the lyre and flutes. But it belongs to political science both to establish a city from the beginning and to use it well when it exists. <gloss>for the city itself</gloss> So it is clear that it would also <margin>Order of <unclear>chapters</unclear></margin> belong to household management both to acquire a house and to use it.

<margin>
Definition of a city.
</margin>

A city, then, is a multitude of houses, lands, and property, sufficient for living well. For it is manifest that if the inhabitants are unable to achieve this, the community <note>original: koinōnia; a fellowship or shared association.</note> happens to be dissolved. Furthermore, it is for this purpose that they come together. That for the sake of which each thing exists and has come into being is also its very essence. Thus it is clear that household management is prior in nature to political science. For its work is prior; for a house is a part of a city. We must therefore consider household management and what its work is. The parts of a house are the human being and property. Since the nature of each thing is first observed in its smallest elements, we must also observe the house in this way...

<summary>This page introduces Aristotle's "Economics," defining the difference between managing a household (a monarchy) and a city (a collective of rulers). It argues that the household is the fundamental building block of the city and must be studied first.</summary>

...commercial, while the third <insert>the</insert> is the Municipal economy <note>original: politikē; refers to the management of a city-state's finances</note>. Of this type, the most excellent revenue is that which comes from the resources belonging to the city within its own territory. Next is the revenue from trade centers and through the transit duties <note>original: epagōgōn en kyklō; likely refers to taxes on goods passing through or around the city's territory</note>. <insert>the</insert> The fourth and final type is the Private economy <note>original: idiōtikē; the management of an individual’s household or estate</note>. This type is irregular because it is not managed toward a single, fixed goal. It is the smallest in scale because both the revenues and the expenditures are modest. Within this type, the best revenue is that which comes from the land; second is that from other types of produce <term>epikarpiōn: profits or yields from assets other than grain, such as orchards or livestock</term>; and third is the revenue from silver <note>likely referring to cash interest or money-lending</note>. Aside from these specific points, there is a principle that is common to all forms of economy, and one must consider it with great care: ensure that expenditures do not become greater than revenues. 

Now that we have stated these divisions, we must next determine whether the administration we are dealing with is a satrapy or a city. We must consider what kind of capacity it has, its current income <note>original: diexodos; the "outlet" or flow of revenue</note>, or its maximum potential, and how these may be utilized. After this, we must examine which types of revenue are entirely missing. Is it possible to make small revenues larger, or to establish entirely new ones? Furthermore, one must consider which expenditures—and how many of them—can be eliminated without causing harm in other areas. We have now spoken about the various economies and their component parts; we shall next discuss the actions taken by those who lived before us.

<margin>Condylus</margin> **C**ondylus, a governor <note>original: ὕπαρχος (*hyparchos*); a subordinate official or lieutenant</note> serving under Mausolus, while passing through the country, was offered a horse as a gift for a festival. He himself also calculated the profits from the trees along the royal roads—both those standing and those that had fallen—and sold their produce. If any of the soldiers saw straight branches and plucked them, he would charge them seven drachmas of equal weight. In this manner, he extracted silver from them.

At the same time, the tax collectors were misleading him as to when a soldier's service might end. He claimed they were <gloss>about</gloss> to be shorn. However, he then suggested that if they each paid a certain sum per head, he would instead send to Greece to fetch hair for the King. They quickly gave him the money.

Aristomenes <note>Aristomenes of Rhodes, an administrator noted for his financial ingenuity</note>, being in need of money for the residents' requirements, held private meetings with each of the two political factions. To the first group, he claimed that the other side was offering to give him money, but since he did not have anyone to whom he would rather entrust the city's affairs than them, he preferred to take from them and hand over the administration of the city to their care. <margin>X</margin> <margin>Charidemus</margin> While Charidemus was holding certain positions in Aeolis <note>a region on the western coast of Asia Minor</note> and Artabazus <note>a Persian satrap who frequently rebelled against the Great King</note> was campaigning against him, he found himself in need of money for his soldiers. # -> Aristotle’s Lectures on Nature, or On Natural Principles, Book I <-

<gloss>The order of scientific instruction</gloss> Since knowing and understanding come about in <gloss>that is, the arts and the sciences</gloss> all methods of inquiry which have <gloss>as the first steps of demonstrations</gloss> <term>principles</term><note>original: "archai"; these are the starting points or foundations of a thing</note>, or <gloss>as the goal or end</gloss> <term>causes</term><note>original: "aitia"; for Aristotle, this includes the reason why something exists</note>, or <gloss>as matter and form</gloss> <term>elements</term><note>original: "stoicheia"; the fundamental components or building blocks</note>, through the recognition of these—(<gloss>this indicates the "why"</gloss> for we believe we know each thing only when we recognize its <gloss>knowledge through the cause</gloss> primary causes, its primary principles, and reach as far as its elements)—it is clear that in the science <gloss>such as the study of nature</gloss> concerning nature, we must <gloss>first</gloss> try to determine <gloss>the progression of beginning and end constitutes the knowledge of clarity</gloss> first the matters regarding its principles. Now, the natural path for us <gloss>nature differs for us</gloss> is to proceed from what is more familiar and clearer to us toward what is clearer and more familiar by nature. <gloss>because while nature is most familiar to us, it is contrary to our own initial knowledge</gloss> For the same things are not familiar to us and familiar in an absolute sense. Therefore, it is necessary to proceed in this way: from things that are less clear by nature but clearer to us, toward things that are clearer and more familiar by nature. To us, the things that are first obvious and <gloss>to our knowledge</gloss> clear are those that are <gloss>rather</gloss> more confused; but later, the principles and elements become known from these by those who distinguish them.

Later, the elements and principles become better known from the things that have occurred, as they <unclear>distinguish</unclear> and divide them.

For to be a thing of a certain quality and a thing of a certain quantity would be one and the same. The later thinkers, just like the ancients, were troubled by this.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Parmenides' theories on the nature of "the One" and "Being." Having previously discussed the logical failures of Melissus, the author now uses Aristotelian logic to demonstrate that "Being" cannot be a single, uniform substance because it must be distinguishable from its accidental qualities.</meta>

<gloss>And why is "precisely being" <note>original: "hoper on" — referring to the essential, fundamental nature of existence itself.</note> not some thing or this specific thing, if indeed the forms are natural?</gloss>
...it is not "precisely being"; nor is there an <gloss>essential nature</gloss> <note>original: "ti ēn einai" — literally "the what it was to be," a technical Aristotelian phrase for the definition or essence of a thing.</note> belonging to it, nor was it anything, nor was it being, not "precisely being." Consider a "man": he is not "white" in an essential way; for if it were so, it would be as if he were "not-being." The color "white" clarifies this: just as with "precisely being," it was not yet possible to say that something is "precisely white"; but this would not signify in the same way that the "essence of white" signifies "precisely being," therefore "being" must signify more than one thing.
Therefore, "being" will not even possess magnitude <note>Magnitude refers to physical size or extension in space.</note>, if indeed "being" is "precisely being." For in such a case, the parts would each have a different being. And that which is "precisely being" is divided into something else which is also "precisely being."

some / how / it is / something
</margin>

And it is reasonably clear: for example, a man is "precisely being" something else, and by necessity "animal" must also be "precisely being," and "two-footed"; for if they are not "precisely being" something, they will be accidents, belonging either to the man or to some other underlying subject <note>original: "hypokeimenō" — the "stratum" or "subject" that possesses qualities.</note>.

<meta>This page continues Aristotle’s analysis of change. Having established that all change requires a subject that persists, he now defines the specific number of "principles" (archai) involved in any process of becoming. He is moving toward his famous triad: matter, form, and privation.</meta>

Therefore, there is a sense in which we should say the **principles** are two, but another sense in which they are three. <summary>Aristotle establishes that every change involves three principles: the underlying matter, the form it acquires, and the privation (the absence of that form) it leaves behind. <meta>This page continues the investigation into whether the natural philosopher should study form, matter, or both. <gloss>the user</gloss>
<gloss>the producer</gloss>

<gloss>The user</gloss> The science that uses a product is the master of the science that produces it; this is the <term>architectonic</term> <note>original: architektonikē; a master-craft or "boss" science that directs other specialized crafts</note> science. <gloss>It [the science]</gloss> <gloss>itself [directs] the productive science</gloss> which is why the science of the "user" is also a kind of master-science. However, they differ in this: the master-science knows the **form** <note>original: eidos; the design, shape, or essential nature</note>, while the productive science knows the **matter** <note>original: hylē; the physical substance or "stuff" things are made of</note>. For instance, the **pilot** <note>original: kybernētēs; the navigator who uses the ship</note> knows and prescribes what the form of the rudder should be, while the shipwright knows from what wood and through what movements it will be constructed. In the realm of art or craft, we create the matter for the sake of the finished work, but in the realm of nature, the matter is already present. Furthermore, matter is a "relative" thing; for a different form, there is a different kind of matter.

To what extent, then, must the student of nature know the form and the essence? Perhaps it is like the doctor knowing the sinew <note>original: neuron; in this era, the word referred to tendons or sinews rather than the modern nervous system</note> or the blacksmith knowing the bronze—knowing them only as far as is necessary to understand what the object is for. This concerns things that have a distinct form but exist within matter. Indeed, as the saying goes, "man is begotten by man and the sun." <note>Aristotle’s way of saying that human life is produced both by a biological parent and the broader life-giving environment of the cosmos</note> How "separable" things exist, and what they are, is a task for **First Philosophy** <note>the branch of study we now call Metaphysics</note> to define.

Now that these things have been determined, we must examine the **causes**, what they are and how many they are in number. Since the purpose of this inquiry is to achieve knowledge, and we do not believe we know a thing until we have grasped the "why" <note>original: to dia ti; literally "the because of what"</note> regarding it.

<summary>Aristotle explains that the "user" of a tool (the master-science) understands its form, while the "maker" understands its matter, and that true scientific knowledge requires grasping the "why" or the cause of a thing.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on the relationship between matter and form to Aristotle’s famous "Four Causes." The text begins a systematic classification of how we explain why things exist or change, continuing the curriculum of natural philosophy.</meta>

Since we must obtain knowledge <gloss>of</gloss> those things concerning causes, it is clearly our task to do so. This applies to birth and destruction <note>original: genesis and phthora; the processes of coming into being and passing away</note> and to every kind of natural change. By knowing their starting points, we can attempt to trace each of our inquiries back to them.

<margin>material cause</margin> In one sense, "cause" is said to be that out of which something comes to be and which persists within it. For example, the **bronze** is the cause of the statue, and **silver** is the cause of the bowl, as are the general categories of these materials.

<margin>formal cause</margin> In another sense, <gloss>formal</gloss> cause is the **form** and the pattern. This is the <term>essential definition</term> <note>original: ho logos ho tou ti ēn einai; literally "the account of the what-it-was-to-be," or the core essence that defines a thing</note>. It also includes the general classes of these definitions. For example, in the case of the **octave** <note>original: dia pasōn; the musical interval</note>, the cause is the ratio of **two to one**; and more broadly, **number** and the various parts contained in the definition.

<margin>efficient cause</margin> Furthermore, cause is that from which the first beginning of **change** or of **rest** originates. For example, the person who has deliberated is a cause, and the **father** is the cause of the child. In general, the **maker** is the cause of the thing made, and that which **initiates change** is the cause of the thing being changed.

<margin>final cause</margin> Finally, cause is the **end** <note>original: telos; the goal or purpose</note>. This is "that for the sake of which" <gloss>the for-the-sake-of-which</gloss> something is done. For example, **health** is the cause of walking. Why does a person walk? We say, "In order to be healthy." In saying this, we believe we have provided the cause. This also applies to all the intermediate steps that occur...

<summary>This page introduces Aristotle's "Four Causes"—material, formal, efficient, and final—which provide a framework for explaining why any natural object or event exists. It uses everyday examples like bronze statues and walking for health to illustrate these philosophical concepts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Aristotle’s critique of the infinite from Physics Book III, Chapter 5. For it is impossible for <term>place</term> <note>original: "topos"; in Aristotelian physics, this is not empty space, but the immediate boundary of the containing body.</note> and body not to correspond. If it were, there would either be a <term>void</term> <note>original: "kenon"; a vacuum or empty space, which Aristotle famously argues cannot exist.</note>, or there would be a body that, by its very nature, exists nowhere.

Anaxagoras, however, speaks strangely regarding the stationarity of the infinite. For he says that the infinite "supports itself," and he bases this on the fact that it is "in itself"—since nothing else contains it—as if to say that wherever a thing is, it is its nature to be there. But this is not true; for a thing might be in a certain location by force <note>Aristotle distinguishes between "natural motion" (like a rock falling) and "enforced motion" (like a rock being thrown upward).</note>, and not where it is naturally inclined to be. 

Therefore, even if it is strictly true that the "whole" does not move—for that which supports itself and is contained within itself must necessarily be motionless—one must still explain *why* it is not natural for it to move. It is not enough to simply state this and be done with it. For anything else might also be unmoved by force, but nothing prevents it from having a natural inclination to move elsewhere. 

Consider the earth: it does not move. Even if the earth were infinite, it would still remain stationary, though it would be held back by the center. It stays there not because there is no other place for it to be carried to, but because it is at the center, and its nature is to be there. And yet one might say that it supports <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the argument that size alone does not explain why something stays still.</note>

<summary>Aristotle argues that physical bodies and the spaces they occupy must correspond in size, and he critiques Anaxagoras for claiming the infinite is stationary simply because it is self-contained.</summary>

For if a body is heavy, its natural motion is toward the center; if it is light, its motion is upward. An infinite body would necessarily have to possess these qualities as well. <margin>itself</margin>

<meta>This page continues Aristotle’s argument from the *Physics* regarding the nature of the infinite. ...tests, it is not that **generation** <note>original: "genesis"; the process of coming into being.</note> or **destruction** <note>original: "phthora"; the process of passing away or ceasing to be.</note> is limited, but rather that one thing is always succeeding another through transformation, while the underlying reality remains. Regarding **additions** and **time**, he says they do not fail or run out in such a way as to leave nothing behind. 

Furthermore, the infinite by **addition** <note>original: "prosthesis"</note> is, in a certain way, the same as the infinite by **division** <note>original: "diairesis"</note>. For within a finite magnitude, addition occurs in an inverse relationship to division. Specifically, as division approaches the infinite (by making parts smaller and smaller), the act of adding those parts back together appears to approach a defined limit. 

For if one takes a finite magnitude and continues to take away parts according to a **constant ratio** <note>For example, always taking half of what remains.</note>—rather than taking the same absolute amount of the whole—one will never actually exhaust the finite magnitude. However, if one increases the amount taken so that he always subtracts the same fixed size every time, he will eventually exhaust the whole. 

Because of this, the finite is not destroyed. In this sense, the **infinite** <note>original: "apeiron"</note> does not exist as a finished whole; rather, it exists in **potentiality** <note>original: "dynamis"</note> and by the process of reduction. 

It also exists in **actuality** <note>original: "entelecheia"; the state of being complete or in operation.</note> in the same way we say a "day" exists or a "contest" exists—as things that are happening. It exists potentially in the same way that **matter** <note>original: "hyle"; the raw "stuff" of the universe which has the potential to become many things but is not any one specific thing on its own.</note> does, and not as an independent, self-subsisting thing like a finite object. 

Even in the case of addition, the infinite exists potentially in this way, which is the same as what we say regarding division; for there is always something of it remaining outside...

...to be infinite, or as they say. For the infinite is not that which has nothing outside of it, but rather that of which there is always <gloss>something</gloss> outside. <meta>This page continues the argument from Physics III.6, where Aristotle defines the "infinite" (apeiron). He has just established that the infinite is not "that which has nothing outside it," but rather "that which always has something outside it." He now moves to correct the common philosophical error of equating the "infinite" with the "whole" or the "all."</meta>

...so it is for the "all." One philosopher claims the infinite is the whole; another that the whole is finite.

### The Infinite and the Whole

Following this, we must recognize that we cannot simply "join linen to linen" <note>original: "linon linō"; a Greek idiom meaning to join like with like, or to try and force two concepts together that do not naturally match.</note> by trying to link the "whole" and the "infinite" to the concept of the infinite itself. It is from this confusion that people attribute a sense of grandeur to the infinite—specifically, the idea that it "contains all things" and "has the all within itself." They say this because the infinite bears a certain resemblance to a "whole."

In reality, the infinite is the **matter** <margin>actuality</margin> <note>The marginal note "actuality" (energeia) likely represents a reader's commentary or a variant reading, as Aristotle's main text argues the infinite is matter/potentiality, not actuality.</note> that allows for the completion of a part. It is a "whole" only **potentially** <term>dynamis: the capacity or potential for being, as opposed to the reality of it</term>, but never in **actuality** <term>entelecheia: the state of being complete or fully realized</term>. It is divisible both by way of reduction <note>That is, dividing a magnitude into smaller and smaller parts indefinitely.</note> and through its opposite, addition.

The infinite is a "whole" and "finite" only in relation to something else, not by its own nature. It contains, but is not itself contained. Because of this, the infinite is **unknowable**, for matter has no **form** <term>eidos: the essence or "look" of a thing that gives it definition</term>.

Consequently, it is evident that the infinite is more properly described as a **part** than as a **whole**. For matter is always a part of the whole, in the same way that bronze is a part of a bronze statue. If the "Great and Small" <note>A reference to Plato’s theory of the "Great and Small" as the material principle of all things.</note> were to contain things in both the physical and the intellectual worlds, it would have to contain the parts as well. Yet, it is both absurd and impossible for that which is unknowable and indefinite to be the thing that contains and defines others. <unclear>ended</unclear>

<summary>Aristotle argues that the infinite is a type of "matter" and a "part" rather than a "whole," because it lacks the form and definition required to be a complete totality. He critiques the idea that the infinite "contains" all things, asserting instead that the infinite is what is "contained" as a potentiality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Aristotle's investigation into the nature of the infinite from Physics, Book III. Having previously argued that the infinite is like "matter" without a final "form," he now explores how infinity operates differently in the realms of addition and division, and why number behaves differently than physical magnitude.</meta>

It follows that addition does not occur in such a way that the infinite seems to exist as a **magnitude** <term>megethos: continuous spatial extension, like a line or a body</term> that exceeds all others. On the contrary, in the case of division, the infinite is contained within a limit, just as **and** <note>original: "kai"; the OCR shows a shorthand version common in manuscripts.</note> form itself is a container. Indeed, the infinite itself is "contained" by form. It is also reasonable that in **number** <term>arithmos: discrete quantity or counting</term> there should be a minimum limit—the unit—while in the direction of the "more," number always exceeds any given plurality. With **magnitudes**, however, the opposite is true: toward the smaller, the division exceeds every magnitude <note>meaning one can always divide a magnitude into something even smaller</note>, while toward the larger, there is no such thing as an infinite magnitude.

The reason for this is that the "one" is indivisible—whatever that "one" happens to be. For example, a man is "one man" and not many. But a **number** is simply a collection of "ones," a certain quantity of them. Therefore, counting must necessarily stop at the indivisible <note>Aristotle believes you cannot have a fraction of a primary unit in pure mathematics; you stop at 1.</note>. Names like "two" and "three" are simply derivative terms, and the same applies to any other number we use. 

However, in the direction of "more," we can always conceive of a higher number, because the potential divisions of a magnitude are infinite.

actuality
</margin>
Thus, the infinite exists **potentially** <term>dynamis: the capacity for something to happen or exist, though it is not currently realized</term>. It is always the case that whatever quantity is taken, the potential for more exceeds any defined plurality. Yet, this infinite number is not something that exists separately from the process of division.

<meta>This page continues Aristotle’s exploration of the infinite in Physics, Book III. He is transitioning from how mathematicians utilize the concept of infinity to a broader philosophical categorization of the infinite as "matter" rather than a "container," concluding with a rebuttal of arguments for an actually existing infinite body.</meta>

Mathematicians do not require the **infinite**, nor do they make use of it; they only require that there be a finite magnitude as large as they wish to assume. On the largest magnitude, it is possible for the same ratio to be divided as in any other magnitude, regardless of its size. 

So, for the purpose of their demonstrations, it makes no difference; however, as for existence, magnitude will exist among real things. <gloss><unclear>but in its being it is of no use for the proof</unclear></gloss> 

Since causes are divided into four types <note>Aristotle's "Four Causes": material, formal, efficient, and final.</note>, it is clear that the **infinite** is a cause in the sense of **matter** <term>hyle: the underlying "stuff" or potential of a thing</term>; and that its essential nature is a **privation** <term>steresis: the absence of a form or quality that should naturally be present</term>. Its underlying subject <term>hypokeimenon: the substrate or "thing" that undergoes change</term> is that which is **continuous** and **perceivable**. 

It appears that everyone else also treats the infinite as if it were matter. Therefore, it is absurd to make the infinite that which **contains**, rather than that which is **contained** <note>Aristotle is critiquing earlier thinkers like Anaximander, who believed the "Infinite" was a divine power that surrounded and governed all things. Aristotle argues it is actually the "part" or the "material" within things.</note>.

It remains to review the arguments according to which the infinite is thought to exist, not only **potentially**, but as something distinct and defined. For some of these arguments do not lead to a necessary conclusion, as they only concern what is possible or **potential**. 

Others have different, true counter-arguments. For instance, it is not necessary for a perceivable body to be **actually** <term>energeia: being in a state of completion or reality</term> infinite simply so that **generation** <term>genesis: the process of coming into existence</term> does not fail or run out. For it is possible for the **destruction** <term>phthora: the process of ceasing to be or decaying</term> of one thing to be the generation of another, even while the whole universe remains finite.

# + Aristotle’s Physics,

In the same way, it is necessary for the natural philosopher <term>physikos: a student of the natural world and its laws</term> to understand the subject of **place**, just as they did regarding the **infinite**—whether it exists or does not, and how it exists, and what it is. For all people suppose that things which exist are "somewhere." Indeed, that which does not exist is "nowhere." For where is a **goat-stag** or a **sphinx**? <note>original: "τραγέλαφος ἢ σφίγξ". Aristotle uses these mythological hybrids to illustrate things that can be imagined but have no physical location because they do not exist.</note> Furthermore, the most common and primary form of **motion** is change in respect to place, which we call **locomotion** <term>phora: movement of a body from one point to another</term>. 

Yet, what place actually is carries many difficulties; for it does not appear the same to those who consider it from all its existing properties. Furthermore, we have nothing handed down from other thinkers that has either previously identified the difficulties or successfully resolved the problems concerning it. That place is indeed "something" seems evident from **displacement** <term>metastasis: the act of one thing being replaced by another in the same space</term>. For where there is now water, once it has gone out as if from a vessel, air is then inside; and at another time, some other body occupies this same place. This, then, of the things that are produced and change—

--- Page 274 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues the inquiry into the nature of "place" (topos). Having previously established that place seems to have a real existence and a specific power (dynamis) in the natural world, Aristotle now turns to the logical difficulties of defining exactly what place is, noting that it shares dimensions with physical bodies but cannot be a body itself.</meta>

We must investigate what **place** is—specifically seeking its <gloss>space</gloss>—and <gloss>it is necessary</gloss> to ask whether it exists, <gloss>whether</gloss> <gloss>what</gloss> <gloss>it</gloss> <gloss>is</gloss>, or if it does not exist at all. Is it a kind of **mass** of a body, or some other **nature**? We must first determine its **genus** <term>genus: the general class or category to which a thing belongs</term>. It possesses three **dimensions**: **length**, **breadth**, and **depth**, which are the same measures by which every **body** is defined. It is impossible, however, for place to be a **body**; for if it were, two bodies would occupy the same space simultaneously. Furthermore, if there is a place and "room" for a body, it follows that there must also be a place for a **surface** and all other **boundaries** <gloss>limits</gloss>. The same reasoning applies here: for where the surfaces of water once were, the surfaces of air will be later. Yet we can find no difference between a **point** and the "place" of a point. Thus, if the place of a point is not something distinct from the point itself, then neither is the place of anything else. For place is not something that exists alongside each of these components. Indeed, what could place even be? Perhaps place does not even exist. For it is neither an **element** <term>element: the basic building blocks of matter, such as air or water</term>, nor is it composed of elements, as a thing with such a nature ought to be. It belongs neither to the **intelligible** <term>intelligible: things known by the mind or intellect, like mathematical concepts</term> nor to the **sensible** <term>sensible: things known through the senses, like physical objects</term>. For while it possesses **magnitude** <note>original: "megethos"</note>, it does not possess a **body**. However, the elements of sensible bodies are themselves bodies; but from "intelligible elements," no physical magnitude can ever arise.

<summary>Aristotle explores the logical paradoxes of "place," arguing that while it has dimensions like a physical body, it cannot actually be a body because two bodies cannot occupy the same space. He questions whether place exists at all, as it fits neither the category of physical matter nor abstract mental concepts.</summary>
<keywords>place, magnitude, dimensions, body vs. space, sensible vs. intelligible, Aristotle's Physics</keywords>

--- Page 275 ---
<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Aristotle began investigating the nature of "place," noting that while it seems to have dimensions like a body, it cannot be a body itself. This page continues the inquiry by testing "place" against the framework of the four causes and addressing the logical paradoxes raised by earlier philosophers like Zeno.</meta>

If place is indeed a specific **category** of existing things, it is difficult to determine its nature. For none of the **four causes** <term>four causes: Aristotle’s framework for explaining why a thing exists, consisting of its material, its form/shape, its starting trigger, and its final purpose</term> can be attributed to it. It does not function as the **matter** of existing things, for nothing is actually composed of "place." It is not the **form** or **definition** of things, nor is it their **end** <term>end: the 'telos' or ultimate purpose toward which a thing moves</term>, and it does not set things in motion.

Furthermore, if place is itself one of the things that exists, where will it be located? Here, **Zeno's paradox** <note>original: "Ζήνωνος ἀπορία" (Zēnonos aporia); Zeno of Elea was a philosopher famous for logical puzzles that suggested motion and space were illusory</note> demands an explanation: for if every existing thing is in a place, then clearly there must also be a **place of the place**, and this will proceed to **infinity**.

Additionally, just as every **body** is in a place, so too in every place there is a body. How, then, shall we explain **things that grow**? From these premises, it would follow that the place must grow along with the things in it, if the place of each thing is neither smaller nor larger than the thing itself.

Because of these problems, we are forced to wonder not only what place is, but even if it exists at all. However, we can say a thing is "in" something else in two ways: either **in its own right** or **in respect to another**. There is **common place**, in which all bodies reside, and **proper place** <gloss>also called primary place</gloss>, which is the immediate space a thing occupies. For example, I might say you are in the **heavens** <note>original: "οὐρανῷ" (ouranō); referring here to the encompassing universe or the sky</note> because you are in the **air**; and this air is in the heavens, just as you are in the air.

<summary>Aristotle explores the logical contradictions of "place," noting it fits none of the four causes and leads to Zeno's infinite regress, before distinguishing between general space and a thing's immediate "primary" place.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Physics, four causes, Zeno's paradox, infinite regress, primary place, common place, philosophy of space</keywords>

--- Page 276 ---
<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Aristotle discussed the paradoxes of place, including Zeno's argument that if every existing thing has a place, place itself must have a place, leading to an infinite regress. He also touched upon how we say things are "in" a location, such as water being in a vessel.</meta>

...that [water is] in the earth. In a similar way, it would seem that place is something. Specifically, since place is that which contains—and contains nothing more than the object itself—the primary container of each body would be its **limit** <term>limit: the 'peras' or boundary where an object ends and something else begins</term>. 

From this perspective, the **form** and the **shape** of each thing would appear to be its place; for the form is the boundary by which the magnitude and the **matter** <term>matter: 'hylē', the underlying 'stuff' or potentiality of a thing before it takes a specific shape</term> of that magnitude are defined. Thus, when we look at it this way, the place of a thing is its **form** <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos); in Aristotle's thought, the 'form' is the essence or defining characteristics of a thing</note>.

However, insofar as place is thought to be the **extension** <term>extension: 'diastēma', the spatial interval or three-dimensional 'stretch' of an object</term> of the magnitude, it is instead thought to be the **matter**. For this extension is something distinct from the magnitude itself; it is that which is contained and defined by the form—just as if it were defined by a surface or a limit. Matter and the **indeterminate** <term>indeterminate: 'aoriston', that which lacks specific boundaries or qualities</term> are of this nature. For if one strips away the limit and the physical qualities of a sphere, nothing remains except the matter.

This is why Plato, in his work the *Timaeus*, says that **matter** and **space** <note>original: "χώρα" (chōra); a term Plato used for the 'receptacle' or 'nurse' of all becoming, where things take shape</note> are the same thing. To him, "that which participates" <note>original: "τὸ μεταληπτικόν" (to metaleptikon); the underlying medium that 'shares' in the eternal Forms</note> and space are one and the same. 

Although he describes "that which participates" differently in the *Timaeus* than he does in his so-called **unwritten doctrines** <term>unwritten doctrines: the 'agrapha dogmata', a collection of Plato's oral teachings known to his students but not included in his formal dialogues</term>, he nevertheless declared that **place** and **space** are the same. Indeed, everyone agrees that place is something that truly exists.

<summary>Aristotle explores whether the "place" of an object should be identified with its "form" (its boundary) or its "matter" (its extension), while noting that Plato equated matter with space.</summary>

--- Page 277 ---
<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Aristotle discussed Plato’s Timaeus, where Plato identified "space" (chōra) and "matter" (hylē) as the same thing. This page continues that investigation, testing whether "place" (topos) can truly be defined as either the form or the matter of an object.</meta>

What matter is, he <note>Referring to Plato</note> alone attempted to describe.

From these considerations, it would seem difficult to discern exactly what **place** <term>place: 'topos', the specific location or 'where' of an object</term> is, if it must be one of these two things—either **matter** or **form**. Especially since these concepts have reached the highest degree of complexity, and it is impossible to understand them in isolation from one another. 

Nevertheless, it is not difficult to see that it is impossible for **place** to be either of these. For **form** <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos)</note> and **matter** <note>original: "ὕλη" (hylē)</note> are not separable from the thing itself, <gloss>thing</gloss> whereas it is possible for a **place** to be separated. For in a space where there was once air, water may (as we say) come to be again; the air and water replace one another. This is true of all other bodies as well. Therefore, **place** is neither a part nor a stable quality of a thing, but is instead something separate from each individual object.

Indeed, **place** seems to be something like a **vessel** <note>original: "ἀγγεῖον" (aggeion); a container like a jar or a bowl</note>. A vessel, in fact, is a "portable place." Yet the vessel is in no way a part of the object it contains.

Insofar, then, as **place** is separable from the thing, it cannot be its **form**; and insofar as it contains the thing, it is something different from its **matter**. For it is generally thought that anything that exists "somewhere" is both a thing in itself and also something distinct from the location it occupies.

<summary>Aristotle argues that place cannot be the "form" or "matter" of an object because place is separable from the object it contains, much like a vessel is separate from its contents.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the discussion of the eight ways something can be "in" another—such as a part in a whole, a species in a genus, or a liquid in a vessel—Aristotle now turns to the logical question of whether it is possible for anything to be "in itself" in a primary sense.</meta>

The remaining point <note>Aristotle is concluding his survey of the linguistic uses of "being in" before defining "place"</note> is this. It is certainly not the case that the container <gloss>original: "in which"</gloss>, the amphora, is sought as being in itself, nor is the wine in itself; rather, it is the **amphora of wine** <term>Amphora of wine: Aristotle treats the combined entity (container + contents) as a single whole to test the logic of self-containment</term> that would be so. For when we speak of both the container and that which is contained, they are both parts of the same whole.

In this sense, then, it is possible for a thing to be in itself; however, in any other sense, it is not possible. For example, we say white is in a body, because the surface is in the body, and the white is in the surface; or that knowledge is in the soul. It is according to these relationships that names are assigned to the parts, as if the thing were in itself. This applies to both the amphora and the wine; when they are separate, they are not a "self," but when they are parts of a whole, they are parts of that single "both." Therefore, a thing is in itself only when we speak of its parts; for instance, white is in a body because it is on the body, and it is in the body because it is on the surface; but when it is in the surface, it is no longer "in" by means of anything else <note>This refers to "primary" presence, where an attribute belongs directly to its subject without an intermediary</note>.

And these two things—the **surface** <term>Surface: 'epiphaneia', the outer limit of a body</term> and the **white**—are different in kind. Each of the two has a distinct nature and power. Indeed, if we look at the matter **inductively** <term>Inductively: 'epaktikōs', reaching a general conclusion by examining specific examples</term>, we see nothing that is "in itself" according to any of the definitions we have established.

Furthermore, by logical argument, it is shown to be impossible. For if a thing were to be in itself, it would be necessary for it to be both things at once: for example, the amphora would have to be both the vessel and the wine, and the wine would have to be both the wine and the amphora, if indeed such a thing were possible.

<summary>Aristotle argues that a thing cannot be "in itself" in a primary sense; it can only be said to be in itself if one of its parts is contained within another of its parts.</summary>
