Indeed, the wine is in that in which <gloss>the</gloss> <gloss>both</gloss> the jar is also present, but it is not the jar itself. Rather, it is there insofar as that container is a jar.

Furthermore, it is clear that their way of being is different. For the definition of the **container** <note>original: "that in which"</note> <unclear>is distinct</unclear>, and the definition of the wine, which is in this container, is also distinct. Moreover, it is not even possible for a thing to be in itself by **accident** <term>Accident: 'symbebēkos', a property that is not part of a thing’s essential definition, such as a man being musical</term>. For if it were, two bodies would be in the same place at the same time. The jar itself would be in itself, if that which is receptive by nature could also be contained within itself.

Additionally, consider if the container were not receptive <unclear>of something else</unclear>, as if wine were contained by wine. It is clear, then, that it is impossible for anything to be in itself in a primary sense.

As for the puzzle raised by **Zeno** <note>Zeno of Elea, famous for his paradoxes; here, he argues that if everything that exists is in a place, then place itself must be in a place, leading to an infinite regress</note>, who wondered if "place" is a thing, it must be in something. There is nothing to prevent the <unclear>primary</unclear> place from being "in" something else, yet not in the sense of being in a physical place. Instead, it is like how **health** <unclear>health</unclear> exists in hot elements as a state, while heat exists in the body as an affection <note>Aristotle distinguishes between a physical location and the way a quality or condition "resides" in a subject</note>. Consequently, there is no necessity for an infinite series of places. One thing is clear: since the place is not the thing within it, but is something else...

<summary>Aristotle concludes that nothing can be "in itself" in a primary sense and resolves Zeno's paradox by explaining that "being in" can refer to properties or states rather than just physical location.</summary>
<keywords>Zeno's paradox, place, container and contained, primary being, infinite regress, accident, state versus affection</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Aristotle concludes the discussion on Zeno's paradox of place and the logical impossibility of a thing being "in itself." He now moves toward a formal definition of place by identifying its essential characteristics and resolving previous contradictions.</meta>

...in a primary sense, both that which is in and that in which it is; and further, there are times when **matter** <term>Matter: 'hyle', the underlying 'stuff' or material substrate of a thing</term> might seem to be place, or at other times **form** <term>Form: 'eidos', the defining shape or essence of a thing</term> might seem to be **place** <note>original: "topos"</note>. Let these matters, then, stand as the puzzles we have worked through. Now, what place actually is might become clear to us if we take up everything that truly seems to belong to it by its own nature. We claim, then, that 
<margin>place</margin>
place is, first, that which **contains** that of which it is the place.

And it is no part of the thing itself. Furthermore, the primary place is neither smaller nor larger than the thing. Additionally, place can be left behind by each object and is **separable** <note>original: "chōriston"; meaning the place remains when the object moves away</note>. In addition to these points, every place has an **up** and a **down** <note>original: "ano kai kato"; Aristotle believed the universe had absolute directions based on its center and circumference</note>. With these principles as our foundation, we must examine what remains. We must try to conduct our investigation in such a way that we provide an account of **what place is** so that the puzzles we have raised are solved, and the characteristics thought to belong to place will indeed be shown to belong to it. Moreover, the cause of the difficulty and of the puzzles surrounding it will then become clear.

<summary>Aristotle transitions from dialectical puzzles to a constructive definition of place, listing its essential properties: it contains objects, is separable from them, and possesses directional qualities (up and down).</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page, Aristotle is refining the definition of place. He has just distinguished between being in something "accidentally" versus "essentially," and is now defining the specific boundary that constitutes a thing's "primary" place.</meta>

...**place** <note>original: "topos"</note> and stable. And it seems to be **primary**. Such is the primary place in which a thing exists. 

Now, when the thing being contained is not **divided** <term>Divided: 'dieiremenon', meaning physically separate or distinct from its surroundings</term> but is instead **continuous** <term>Continuous: 'syneches', meaning the parts are joined so they share a single limit or boundary</term>, it is not said to be "in" that container as if in a place; rather, it is as a **part in a whole**. 

But when a thing is divided and merely **touching**, it is primarily in the **extremity** <note>The "eschaton" or the innermost boundary of the container</note> of the surrounding container. This boundary is neither a part of the thing within it, nor is it larger than the **extension** <note>original: "diastematos"; the volume or space occupied by the object</note> of the thing, but is exactly **equal** to it. Furthermore:
*   If a thing is **continuous** with its surroundings, it does not move *in* them, but moves *with* them. 
*   If a thing is **divided**, it moves *in* its surroundings. 

This remains true whether the container itself is in motion or not. To clarify, when something is not divided, it is spoken of as a **part in a whole**, such as **sight** <gloss>the faculty of vision</gloss> in the **eye**, or the **hand** in the **body**. But when it is divided, it is like **water in a bucket** or **wine in a ceramic jar**. For the hand moves *with* the body, but the water moves *within* the bucket.

It is now clear from these observations what place is. <summary>Aristotle defines "primary place" as the immediate, equal boundary of a container and distinguishes between being a "part" of a whole versus being "in" a place based on whether an object is continuous with or separated from its surroundings.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the existence of "the void." For, thinking that "being" is "place" and that "place" is a body, they claim that where there is absolutely nothing, that is the **void**; consequently, they believe that what is full of air is also void. It is not this, then, that needs to be shown—that air is something—but rather it must be shown that there is no **interval** <term>extension</term><note>original: "diastema," referring to a spatial gap or distance between points</note> distinct from bodies, which is either separable or exists in actuality, and which breaks up the totality of body so that it is not **continuous** <note>original: "syneches," meaning a single, unbroken physical whole</note>. <margin>the rest</margin> Now, these thinkers do not meet the problem "at the front door" <note>original: "ou kata thyras," a Greek idiom meaning they do not address the core of the issue directly</note>; but those who claim the void exists do so more effectively. This includes both **locomotion** <term>movement from place to place</term> and **growth**; for it seems that motion could not exist unless there were a void. For they argue that it is impossible for that which is full to receive anything into it. If it could receive something, and two bodies could be in the same place, then it would be possible for any number of bodies to exist together at once. However, one would then be unable to explain the distinction that allows the aforementioned movement to occur. And if this were possible, then even the **smallest** thing could receive the largest.

<summary>Aristotle clarifies that the debate over the "void" is not about whether air is a substance, but whether a spatial gap exists independently of matter. He outlines the arguments of the Atomists, who claim that motion and growth would be impossible without such empty spaces.</summary>

The same reasoning will naturally apply to the void regarding the concepts of **up** and **down**; for those who say the void exists treat it as a **place**. And indeed, how will a body exist in it, or in a place?

<meta>This page continues Aristotle's examination of the "void." He previously argued that the arguments for its existence (based on growth and the ash experiment) were flawed. ...in the **void**. For it also follows that when a whole is placed as if in a **separate and persistent place**, a problem arises. For a part of a body, if it is not separated from the whole, will not be in a specific "place" of its own, but rather within the whole. And if there is no such thing as "place," then there will be no **void** <term>empty space</term> <note>original: "kenon"</note> either. 

Furthermore, to those who argue that a void is a necessary condition if there is to be **motion** <term>movement or change</term> <note>original: "kinēsis"</note>, the opposite conclusion follows if one examines the matter closely: it is impossible for even a single thing to move if a void exists. 

Just as some claim that the **earth** remains at rest because of its uniformity <note>Aristotle is likely referring to Anaximander's theory that the Earth stays in the center of the universe because it is equidistant from all points and thus has no reason to move in one direction over another.</note>, it is likewise necessary to remain at **rest** <note>original: "ēremein"</note> in a void. This is because there is no reason for an object to move more or less in one direction than another; insofar as a thing is "void," it possesses no distinctions <note>original: "diaphoran"</note> or directional differences.

First, we must understand that every motion is either **forced** <note>original: "biā"</note> or **natural** <note>original: "kata physin"</note>. If there is forced motion, there must necessarily be natural motion as well; for forced motion is that which is "against nature," and what is against nature is secondary to what is natural. Therefore, if the **natural bodies** <note>the fundamental elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note> do not possess a natural motion, then none of the other types of motion can exist at all. 

But how can there be any "natural" motion if there are no distinctions of direction within the void or the **infinite**? <note>Aristotle's point is that natural motion requires a destination—fire moves "up" and earth moves "down." In a void, which is by definition empty and featureless, there is no "up" or "down," leaving an object with no natural direction to travel.</note>

The natural path of knowledge proceeds from what is more known to us and <gloss>the path of knowledge</gloss> clearer, toward what is clearer by nature and more <gloss>but more obscure to us</gloss> known. For the same things are not known to us and known in an absolute sense. Therefore, it is necessary to proceed in this way: from things that are more obscure by nature but clearer to us, toward things that are clearer and more known by nature. It introduces the famous Aristotelian method of learning: moving from general, "confused" sensory impressions to specific, organized natural principles.</summary>

For it is not separate: Parmenides had not yet seen the whole <note>Aristotle suggests Parmenides' view was incomplete because he did not distinguish between different ways a thing can "be."</note> all at once. For if one assumes that "being" signifies only one thing of whatever it is predicated, then it must be both "what essentially is" <term>hoper on; the core essence of a thing, what it is in itself</term> and "what essentially is one." But an "accident" <term>symbebekos; an attribute that is not part of a thing's core definition, such as being 'musical' or 'white'</term> is spoken of as belonging to some underlying subject. So, the subject to which "being" is an accident will not "be" at all. For if it is something different from "being," then "being" would effectively be "not-being." Therefore, "what essentially is being" would not even be present in it. For "being" cannot be an attribute of itself, especially since "being" signifies many different things in such a way that each is a distinct something. And it is assumed that "being" signifies "one" in this sense: that "what essentially is being" is not an accident of anything. For if "what essentially is being"...

<margin>
...that the white is, nothing that is essentially being. For it is not even an accident.
</margin>

...signifies "white," and if then "what essentially is being" itself were to be "white," its essence would be one and the same. For nothing is "what essentially is being" if it is not "white" itself. For in that way it is just like "white." At the same time, however, nothing exists which is "what essentially is being" that is not also "one." This is why saying "this is white" does not signify [absolute] being. Consequently, "white" also signifies "what essentially is being." Therefore, "being" signifies more than one thing. Furthermore, "being" will not even have magnitude <note>size or physical extension</note>, if indeed being is only "what essentially is being." For the essence of each of the parts would be different from the whole: — 

<margin>
...to be separate, the name is "what essentially is being." And "what essentially is being" exists according to substance <note>ousia</note>. Since being "one" is known from that source in which the name resides.
</margin>

<image-desc>red ornamental circle with a center dot, used as a paragraph marker</image-desc> Furthermore, that which is "what essentially is being" appears to be divisible into other things that are also "what essentially is being" in their own definition. For example, if "man" is "what essentially is being," it is necessary that "animal" is also "what essentially is being" and that "two-footed" is as well. For if they are not "what essentially is being," they must be mere accidents. They would be accidents either to the "man" or to some other underlying subject. But this is impossible. We define an accident as something that "may or may not belong"...

<summary>Aristotle refutes Parmenides' claim that "Being is One" by demonstrating that "being" must have multiple meanings, distinguishing between a thing's essential nature and its accidental attributes. He argues that if being were only one thing, definitions (like "man is a two-footed animal") would become logically impossible.</summary>

<summary>This page outlines Aristotle's survey of early Greek physical theories, distinguishing between those who derive many things from one via density/rarity (like Anaximenes) and those who believe opposites are separated out from a primordial mixture (like Anaximander and Anaxagoras).</summary>

--- Page 320 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "physicists" (early natural philosophers), moving from the general problem of change to the specific theories of Anaxagoras. It examines his radical idea that "everything is in everything" and Aristotle’s initial objections regarding the possibility of scientific knowledge under such a system.</meta>

->Since Anaxagoras says that coming-to-be is actually alteration, combination, and separation, and asks how the other theories could not be the same<-
->He says that nothing is truly born or destroyed, but rather things are separated out from existing things that were already mixed together.<-

<margin>
Note how Anaxagoras says that "coming-to-be" <note>original: γένεσις (genesis)</note> is actually "alteration" <note>original: ἀλλοίωσις (alloiosis); a change in quality rather than a change in essence.</note>.
</margin>

It follows, then, that alterations also occur—such as judgment <note>The scribe likely means "separation" (krisis) here, following the theme of the text.</note>, combination, and separation. **Furthermore**, if we assume that coming-to-be cannot happen from "non-being" (nothingness), then things must already exist within the mixture simultaneously. This entire line of reasoning assumes that it is necessary for things to arise either from "being" or from "non-being." However, coming to be from non-being is impossible. On this specific opinion, all those who study nature <note>The "physiologoi" or natural philosophers who preceded Aristotle.</note> are in agreement. Consequently, they believed it followed by necessity that things are born from existing things that are already present within, but due to the smallness of their mass, they are invisible to us. For this reason, they claim that "everything is mixed in everything," because they saw everything coming-to-be out of everything. But things appear different from one another and are called by different names based on whatever most exceeds the others in the mixture of infinite parts. Nothing is purely and entirely white, or black, or sweet, or flesh, or bone; but whatever each thing contains the most of, that is thought to be the "nature" of the thing.

<margin>
Consider if the "like-parts" <note>original: ὁμοιομερῆ (homoiomerê); substances like gold or flesh where any piece of the whole is the same substance as the whole.</note> are indeed flesh, and bits of gold come from gold, and liquids from liquids; but while some are obvious among existing things, others are hidden to most people.
</margin>

<margin>
Regarding the idea that the number of "principles" <note>original: ἀρχῶν (archai); the fundamental building blocks of reality.</note> is infinite: because the infinite has no "form" <note>original: εἶδος (eidos)</note>, it is not possible for it to be fully known.
</margin>

**If** indeed it is necessary that everything be either infinite or limited, then if the quantity is infinite, it is an unknown quantity; and if it is infinite in kind <note>In its "species" or "form."</note>, it is an unknown quality. If the principles are infinite in both number and kind, it is impossible to know the things made from them. We only suppose we "know" a composite thing when we know what parts and how many parts it is made from.

<margin>
All the "like-parts" <note>homeomerous substances</note> are infinite in number, and the "infinite" is, by definition, the "unknown."
</margin>

**Furthermore**, if it is possible for a part of a certain body to be of any size whatsoever in terms of magnitude or smallness <note>Aristotle is arguing against the idea that you can just keep dividing or expanding things forever without changing their nature.</note>, it is clear that the living animal itself cannot be of just any size. This will be equally clear regarding the parts...

<margin>
Everything comes to be from everything, just as with "participles" <note>A grammatical metaphor used by the commentator to explain how one thing "shares" in the identity of another.</note> if we name the greatest thing by its greatest component.
</margin>

<margin>
Take Anaxagoras for example: he says that in the beginning, everything was "one" whole; then, it entered a state where everything is mixed.
</margin>

<summary>Aristotle explains Anaxagoras’s theory that matter is an infinite mixture where "everything is in everything," and begins to critique it by arguing that an infinite number of principles would make the natural world impossible to truly know or define.</summary>
<keywords>Anaxagoras, coming-to-be, alteration, mixture, infinity, like-parts, homeomery, principles of nature, scientific knowledge</keywords>

**If** indeed all things exist within every other thing, and they are born and come to be from that mixture, being separated <note>original: ἐκκρινόμενον (ekkrinomenon); the process of "secretion" or "separation out" from a mixture.</note> from a larger quantity; and if the substance from which they are made is produced in this way—for instance, water being secreted from flesh, and flesh from water—and if a finite body <note>A body with specific boundaries or limits.</note> loses a finite part, it is clear that it is impossible for everything to exist in everything. For if flesh is extracted from water, and then more flesh is produced from the remaining water, the water will eventually be used up. Even if the piece removed is always smaller than the one before, it still cannot shrink below a certain size. Therefore, if the extraction stops, then not everything was in everything to begin with; for in the remaining water, no more flesh exists. However, if the extraction never stops but always allows for another piece to be removed, then a finite magnitude would contain an infinite number of finite parts. This is impossible <note>Aristotle is pointing out a mathematical absurdity: you cannot fit an infinite number of pieces of a specific minimum size into a container that has a fixed, finite size.</note>.

great absurdity.

**I**n addition to these points, if every body must necessarily become smaller when a part is removed from it, and if the quantity of flesh is defined by a specific maximum and minimum size, it is clear that from a piece of flesh of the smallest possible size, no further body can be extracted; for that extracted piece would have to be smaller than the minimum possible size.

<margin>
† The infinite in magnitude exists, yet the magnitude cannot be increased.
</margin>

**F**urthermore, in these "infinite bodies" <note>Anaxagoras's seeds or the "everything in everything" mixture.</note>, there would already have to exist infinite flesh and blood; though they would be separated from each other, they would already be actual substances <note>original: οὐσία (ousia)</note>, and from each one <unclear>life would be generated</unclear>.

# One must not be ignorant

<margin>

->As it is held among the ancients, so is my own perspective. It is possible that no one can perceive any of those things of such great magnitude through suspicion alone. Since they differ from the same <unclear>things</unclear>. They create an absolute separation of form-making.<-

The claim that something is never in a certain state is not said reasonably, though it is said correctly in another sense. For the properties <term>passions: the original Greek *pathe* refers to the qualities, attributes, or "affections" of a substance—such as color or heat—rather than human emotions</term> are inseparable from the substance. If, then, our sight corresponds to colors, then they say opposites exist there. But this would not be the case for those who are healthy. It is not a different thing, nor does it exist apart from a subject. Thus, it is absurd to think that a state is impossible simply because nature does not wish to be disposed that way. To do the impossible is to fail even to hypothesize what kind of thing it is. For if it were of a certain kind, it would not be magnitude itself. For of whatever kind it might be, one would have to separate the properties from the object. <margin>Since properties are nothing other than the magnitudes themselves existing in a certain way, it would be as if someone claimed to separate the properties from the magnitude itself.</margin> <note>The scribe uses a red initial "T" and red marks for emphasis or new sections.</note> Nor does he correctly understand knowledge as being of a single kind. It is as different as the sun is from a cave. <gloss>The cave likewise</gloss> is divided, but it is not the same. For the method is not the same as those who set out the plans for houses and dwellings; nor do fire and air simply arise out of them. <margin>The sun represents the sensible object; the cave represents the sense organ <note>original: αἰσθητήριον (aistheterion)</note>; knowledge is not divided in the same way between them.</margin> It is easy to grasp the flaw regarding the mixture which Empedocles <note>Empedocles (c. 490–430 BCE) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that all matter is composed of four roots: earth, air, fire, and water.</note> proposes. What then does he say? Those who claim that the Whole is one and unmoving use the same principles. For Parmenides <note>Parmenides (early 5th century BCE) argued that reality is a single, unchanging "Being."</note> makes "Hot" and "Cold" his principles. These he identifies as Fire and Earth. He also uses "Rare" and "Dense." And Democritus <note>Democritus (c. 460–370 BCE) was a pioneer of atomic theory, suggesting the world is made of "atoms and void."</note> posits the "Solid" and the "Void," of which he says one is *Being* and the other is *Non-being*. Furthermore, he distinguishes things by their position, shape, and order. For these are the categories of opposites. In terms of position: up and down, forward and backward. In terms of shape: the angle, the straight line, and the curved. Whoever, therefore, establishes principles through all these things, it is clear. And they themselves irrationally claim that the principles do not arise from one another, nor...

<header>An assessment of sight through passive quality. Valuing through opposites. What [comes] from ten or the eye from opposites.</header>

<margin>
Since first it seems to all that there is no one who does not assume contraries, but all set contraries as <term>principles: *archai*, the fundamental starting points or elements of reality</term>; some setting heat and cold, others wet and dry... <note>original: "ἐπεὶ πρῶτον μὲν πᾶσι δόξαι..." This is a paraphrase of Aristotle's *Physics* 188a.</note>
</margin>

...from one another, and from these, all things [come to be]. These things belong to the first contraries. On account of their being, they do not come from one another. On account of their nature, they do not come from one another.
<gloss>these things are known</gloss>
**B**ut it is necessary to consider this in other cases as well, to see how it happens. One must first grasp that of all things that exist, nothing is naturally fit to act upon, nor to be acted upon by, just anything at random. Nor does anything come into being from just anything, unless one is speaking <term>accidentally: *kata symbebekos*, a logical term for a property that is not essential to the thing's nature, like a builder being musical</term>. For how could "white" come from "musical"? Unless "musical" happened to be an accidental property of the "white" or the "black" object. Instead, "white" comes from "not-white"—and not from just anything "not-white," but specifically from "black" or the <term>intermediates: *metaxy*, the shades like grey that exist between two extremes</term>. Nor indeed does "musical" come from "not-musical," but again, not from just anything; it comes from the "unmusical" or whatever might be between them. And when something is destroyed, it does not pass into just anything; "white" does not perish into "musical," but into "not-white"—that is, into "black" or an intermediate shade. Similarly, "musical" perishes into "not-musical," and specifically into the "unmusical" or an intermediate state. This is likewise the case for all other things. For even those things that are not simple, but composite, follow the same logic.

<margin>
Disorder and lawlessness are from contraries, so that even the principles...

We are able, therefore, to argue whether there are two, three, or more principles. It is not possible for there to be only one, for opposites are not one. And "substance" or being is itself a single genus. # † Aristotle, Book Four:

<margin>
Place
</margin>
In the same way, it is also necessary for the **natural philosopher** <note>original: *physikon*; one who studies nature or "physics."</note> to have knowledge concerning **place** <note>original: *topos*; the specific location or space occupied by an object.</note>, namely whether it exists or <unclear>not</unclear>. 

Furthermore, of all the types of **motion** <note>original: *kinēseōs*; in Aristotle's work, this term encompasses all forms of change, including growth and alteration, not just movement through space.</note>, the most common and most fundamental is motion with respect to place, which we call **locomotion** <note>original: *phora*; the movement of an object from one point to another.</note>. This is because everyone supposes that things which exist are "somewhere." However, the study of **place** has been left with many **difficulties** <note>original: *aporiai*; philosophical puzzles or contradictions that arise when trying to define a concept logically.</note>. For instance, in the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato; Aristotle here refers to Plato’s attempt to define space or "the receptacle" in that work.</note>, place is identified with matter.

<meta>This page appears to shift focus from the discussion of "place" in Book IV of Aristotle’s Physics (mentioned on the previous page) to a summary of natural principles and the history of early Greek philosophy. It specifically references Aristotle’s definition of "nature" from Physics Book II and then catalogs the "first principles" identified by the Presocratic thinkers.</meta>

...in which there is a **principle of motion and rest**, in which it exists primarily of itself <gloss>// Physics Book II, Ch. 1.</gloss> and not by accident. And these are the things which do not perish of necessity, being things that exist by nature.

Those following **Aristotle** and **Plato** believe that a **principle** <note>original: *archē*; the starting point, cause, or underlying governing rule of a thing.</note> and an **element** <note>original: *stoicheion*; the basic material components, like the letters of an alphabet.</note> differ. The principle seems to belong to form and essence, while the element belongs to the category of material elements. In combination with these, one also considers things that are animate <note>original: *empsychōn*; "en-souled" or living beings.</note> or inanimate.

Among these, **Empedocles** is considered most sacred, as he was also among the ancients <gloss>note in manuscript!</gloss>, for identifying the principle of the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>.

As for the history of philosophy, so that it might be known, there came **Thales of Miletus** the elder; he is thought to have begun philosophy, and from him the **Ionian school** <note>original: *hairesis*; a "sect" or specific tradition of thought.</note> received its name. This Thales is recorded in these same accounts: Thales, then, says that the principle of generation is **water**. Why? Because all plants are naturally moist and bear fruit, whereas dried things never do. He argued this because even the sun is rekindled from the moisture of the sea, as is the cosmos itself. He was the first, as they say, to claim that everything is made of water.

But **Anaximander** says it is the **infinite** <note>original: *apeiron*; the "unbounded" or "limitless" substance that precedes the elements.</note>, and from this all things come to be and into it they are destroyed, so that the process of generation never fails the underlying substance. He declares whether this infinite is fire, or water, or other things.

**Anaximenes**, however, says it is **air**. He claims the underlying substance is a single thing, like the cosmos. For spirit <note>original: *pneuma*; breath or life-force.</note> holds us together and encompasses these things. But it is impossible for a single whole principle of all beings to be everything—how could it be? Rather, is it not the "maker," or the sun and the air, or mobile fire?

**Anaxagoras of Clazomenae** declared the **homeomeries** <note>original: *homoiomereiai*; "parts that are like the whole." Anaxagoras believed that matter is made of tiny seeds that contain the qualities of the whole (e.g., blood is made of tiny drops of blood).</note>. For it seemed to him a difficulty <note>original: *aporia*; a philosophical puzzle.</note> that anything should come from what in no way exists, or be destroyed into non-existence. Therefore, from the food we consume, blood is formed, and the rest, for the parts within us increase. All things that exist are potentially in the food. And he called these "homeomeries" the whole. He said, "All things were together," but in a certain way; or he says all existing things were together like certain colors. But **Mind** <note>original: *Nous*; the cosmic intelligence or intellect.</note> separated and ordered them. He is to be accepted because he joined the physical elements to the concept of Mind. These "homeomeries" consist of things like veins and their specific parts, and he brings Mind together with these homeomeries.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ancient philosophical systems. Having concluded the section on Pythagoras on the previous page, the text now transitions into the "pluralist" school of Empedocles, the "Idealism" of Socrates and Plato, the "Stoicism" of Zeno, and finally the "Atomism" and ethics of Epicurus, followed by a general physical theory of how the universe formed.</meta>

And [the universe is] impassive, without a void: <insert>+</insert> **Empedocles**, son of Meton, from Akragas <note>Modern Agrigento in Sicily.</note>, held that there are **elements** <note>original: *stoicheia*; the fundamental building blocks of matter.</note>. He named two principles as powers: **Love** <note>original: *Philia*; the force of attraction and unification.</note> and **Strife** <note>original: *Neikos*; the force of repulsion and division.</note>. He says the one brings about unification, and the other division. He calls them the "Four Roots of all things." Hear them: **Zeus** <note>Zeus here represents the element of Fire or the bright Ether.</note>, the ether; **Hera**, the life-bearer <note>Hera represents the element of Earth.</note>; **Aidoneus** <note>Hades, representing the element of Air.</note>; and **Nestis**, who with her tears wets the mortal spring <note>Nestis represents the element of Water.</note>. 

**Socrates**, son of Sophroniscus, and **Plato**, son of Ariston, sought the following regarding the **principles** <note>original: *archai*; the starting points of reality.</note>: **God**, **Matter**, and the **Idea** <note>The "Forms" or perfect blueprints of things.</note>. These truly exist. The substrate <note>The underlying material world.</note> possesses both coming-into-being and destruction. The **Idea** is a certain incorporeal **substance** <note>original: *ousia*; the essential being of a thing.</note> residing in the thoughts of God. Wherein God is the Mind of the world, and is incorporeal. He also speaks of **Matter**. There are four elements, and the solid body is ethereal and unchangeable. 

**Zeno**, son of Mnaseas, the Cypriot <note>The founder of the Stoic school.</note>, viewed the principles as the **Active** <note>original: *poietikan*; the creative force or Logos.</note> and the **Matter** that is acted upon. He also speaks of elements: from which water, earth, and [the others] are chosen. 

**Pythagoras** held that the principles participated in the One. **Epicurus** thought that the study of "Ideas" should not even be recognized. He makes the **goal** <note>original: *telos*; the ultimate purpose of life.</note> of his system **pleasure** <note>original: *hedone*; which Epicurus defined as the absence of pain and fear.</note>. Or, as his interpreters explain, the state of theology <note>A divine-like state of tranquility.</note>, not an impure one. But for this reason, the other philosophers reject him. 

They speak of the moon as if it were a kind of earth, and they bring up its variety and certain differences occurring [on its surface]. Just as under a shadow, it is somehow distinguished by its richness, even if it is filled with mind. As a living goal, so it lived around the yawning gaps and the formation of the **spirit** <note>original: *pneumatos*; breath or animating force.</note>. Driven by the sharp North Wind, the "bringer of bright skies," it moves in circles. Because of the clearing of the northern part, it was composed in a circular shape for them: an analysis of those things having motion, moving continuously, and because of this, [it is] often Mother Earth. 

When these things were gathered within it, the larger and **heaviest** <unclear>parts</unclear> settled at the bottom. But the small, round, and easily-moved parts stood out; such things were carried toward the heavens. For how did the uplifting power fail? But since the [elements] were carried in a vessel, they were intertwined with one another. And by their refraction, they created things together, and then toward the heavens, outside of these, the stars [were formed]. A multitude of the spirits being struck at the extremities, it became energized by the spirit. Being thus filled with spirit, it carried the stars around with it. Under the weight of the heavy things, the earth was formed, but from the heavenly things came fire and air, and much matter.

...mentions: the Monad is the world and **<term>God</term>** <note>original: *theos*; here referring to the primary divine principle</note>. **Anaximander** says the celestial stars are gods. **Democritus** says Mind is **<term>God</term>**, being in a fire-like form as the soul of the world. **Pythagoras** calls the Monad [God]; one part is the Good and the One, while the other is a demon and evil. **<term>Idea</term>** <note>A "Form" or "Blueprint"—the perfect non-physical pattern of a thing.</note> is an incorporeal substance; it does not exist by itself, but it gives image to the shapes of matter and becomes the cause of their manifestation. **Socrates** and **Plato** say these are separate, existing in the thoughts of the Mind. **Aristotle** accepted forms and ideas, yet not as things separated from matter. **The Stoics** following Zeno say that Ideas are merely our own mental concepts. **Plato** says that only one world was made, as it corresponds to the world itself. Nature is the result.

The **mathematicians** <note>original: *mathematikoi*; scholars who applied numerical ratios to astronomy</note> say the sun is a precursor, calling it the "Morning Star" <note>original: *heōsphoron*; the "dawn-bringer"</note> which goes before all. The air, for the same reason, is as the air is. And there are destructions and wanderings through it. The **Stoics** [say] the world itself and the stars are [formed] from exhalations. +

### On the size of the sun.

**Eudoxus** <note>original: *Eudoxos*; a famous 4th-century BCE astronomer and mathematician</note> [follows] Aratus.
Commonly, [the sun appears] to be a cubit's width <note>about 18 inches; a common ancient way to describe the sun's apparent size in the sky</note> to the stars. Those who are without signs upon a tomb. **Epicurus** <note>original: *Epikouros*; he argued that our senses are the primary source of truth, so the sun must be roughly the size it appears to be</note> says it is either exactly as it appears or slightly larger or smaller. **Anaximander** <note>original: *Anaximandros*; the first to suggest the sun was a massive physical object</note> [says] it is a circle that is twenty-fold <note>doxographical tradition usually records this as 27 or 28 times</note> the size of the earth, having [the shape of] a chariot wheel. He says the sun is like a hollow [wheel] full of fire. And through a certain part of an appearing opening, the fire [bursts out], just as if through the pipe of a bellows-nozzle <note>original: *prēstēros*; used here to describe the pressurized release of fire</note>. From this, the sun is produced. [Others say it is] from fiery clouds. The **Stoics** [say] it is a god [nourished] from the exhalation of the air. When these are gathered together, the sun is formed from fiery clouds. The **Stoics** [also call it] an intellectual ignition <note>original: *anamma noeron*</note> from the sea. [Others say it is] from the greatest fire. **Anaxagoras**, **Democritus**, and **Metrodorus** [say it is] a red-hot mass <term>red-hot mass: *mudron*; a lump of burning metal or stone</term>, or a fiery stone. [Others say it is] a spherical form from the "fifth body" <note>the ether, the pure substance of the heavens</note>. **Philolaus the Pythagorean** <note>original: *Philolaos*; the first to propose that the Earth is not the center of the universe</note> [says it is] glass-like, receiving the brilliance of the fire in the world. It sends out warmth and light. # Commentary on the First Book of Aristotle’s *On the Soul*

<margin>
Commentary on the first book of Aristotle's *On the Soul* <note>original: "De Anima"; the shorthand "π' ψ' χ'" in the Greek stands for *Peri Psychēs*, the work's Greek title</note>
</margin>

The powers of the soul are of two kinds: some are vital, while others are cognitive. Among souls, some are vital and appetitive <note>referring to the soul's desires or drives</note>, while others are cognitive. Similarly, these are divided again; specifically, the cognitive powers must be divided into opinion, discursive reason, and intellect. Now, opinion concerns the universal as it exists within sensible things <note>objects that can be perceived by the five senses</note>. For it knows that we will see every fire as hot, and that every human is two-footed. It also deals with things known by the intellect; it knows, for instance, the conclusion that every soul is immortal. Yet, it no longer knows *why* it is immortal. Perhaps opinion and the intellect are considered together because conclusions do not remain fixed. Why the soul is immortal is not a matter for opinion, but for discursive reason <note>original: *dianoia*; the step-by-step process of logical thinking</note> to address. 

Hence, in this regard, they define opinion by saying that while facts remain, we say that discursive reasons "cut through" them. For when discursive reason has formulated a syllogism <note>a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note> that the soul is immortal, the conclusion alone is what we call opinion. Discursive reason is <unclear>necessary</unclear> to travel a certain path, moving from <unclear>premises</unclear> to a conclusion, from which its motion <unclear>arises. And</unclear> this is the work of discursive reason. But the work of the intellect <note>original: *nous*; the faculty of immediate, intuitive understanding</note> is an <unclear>effortless</unclear> strike, better than demonstration, which it <unclear>applies</unclear> to things. Just as the sense of sight, having <unclear>grasped</unclear> perhaps a white color or a particular shape, has a knowledge of it that is better <unclear>than a demonstration</unclear>. For it has no need <unclear>for these things</unclear> of a syllogism. The activity of the intellect <unclear>is drawn along</unclear> by unchanging things, as if having reached the peak of purification and <unclear>attained</unclear> science, and through the purifying virtues, <unclear>having snatched away</unclear> through a state of passionlessness <note>original: *apatheia*; not "indifference," but a state of being undisturbed by the emotions</note>, it will be saved to do good by its vital and <unclear>cognitive</unclear> power.

<summary>This page introduces a commentary on Aristotle's "On the Soul," categorizing the soul's faculties into vital and cognitive powers. It distinguishes between opinion (knowing a fact), discursive reason (logical processing), and intellect (direct, intuitive understanding).</summary>

--- Page 374 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded with a discussion on how the soul transitions from simple opinion—knowing that something is true—to discursive reason, which understands the logical "why" behind a fact. This page continues that hierarchy, explaining how the soul moves from the physical world toward the contemplation of divine, immaterial truths.</meta>

For when the soul's faculties exist together, the most perfect state occurs for those who have been set apart toward the things that truly exist. While discursive reason <note>original: *dianoia*; the soul's ability to think through a problem step-by-step</note> concerns itself with things that can be reasoned through, opinion concerns things that are merely objects of opinion. Among these powers, the intellect <note>original: *nous*; the highest form of direct, intuitive understanding</note> holds its rank [at the top], while opinion is the lowest, and discursive reason is the middle. This middle power is uniquely suited to our human soul, since our soul itself holds the middle rank in the universe <note>placed between the purely divine/intellectual realm and the purely physical/sensory realm</note>. And through this discursive reason, I say, our soul is led upward to the contemplation <note>original: *theoria*; a deep, focused looking at truth</note> of true beings, which is the perfection of the soul.

For because our soul is both nurtured with and naturally tied to things perceived by the senses, it is at first unable—due to its habituation to these sensible things—to arrive at the contemplation of intellectual and immaterial things. For the soul imagines that those higher things also possess bodies, and it visualizes there whatever it sees among the objects of the senses. As <term>Plato</term> <note>the famous Greek philosopher and teacher of Aristotle</note> says in the <term>Phaedo</term> <note>Plato’s dialogue on the soul and its journey after death</note>, this is the most difficult thing for us: that whenever we manage to take even a brief rest from the demands of the physical body and <unclear>to those</unclear> <unclear>wish</unclear> to examine something by <unclear>taking up</unclear> the contemplation of divine things, the imagination <note>original: *phantasia*</note> intrudes and disturbs us. It moves us to suspect that divine things are physical bodies and that they possess size and shape. 

The imagination does not allow us to think about them in an incorporeal <note>without a physical body</note> and shapeless way. For this reason, the soul traveling toward its own perfection must move toward intellectual things via discursive reason, which deals with the "middle" level of reality. Such objects of reason are things like our own soul and the study of the soul itself. Furthermore, this includes mathematics; these mathematical objects possess an immaterial essence <note>original: *ousia*; their definitions do not require matter</note>, even if they do not possess an independent [immaterial] existence <note>original: *hyparxis*; referring to the idea that numbers and shapes are usually found within physical objects rather than floating freely</note>.

<summary>This page describes the hierarchy of the soul's cognitive powers—intellect, reason, and opinion—and explains why the human soul struggles to contemplate divine truths due to its attachment to the physical body and imagination.</summary>

This point is sacred regarding the **Moon**. For it says that in the case of things that share the same substance <note>original: *homoousia*; things of the same fundamental nature or essence</note>, as it is with one, so it must necessarily be with all. All the stars are of the same substance. Since it has been demonstrated that the moon is spherical, it is clear then that the other stars will also be spherical. In the same way, one who sees **smoke** reasons that **fire** lies beneath that place. If such a person already knows that all smoke comes from fire, this entire conclusion comes from the fire. 

Just so, as I said, it is possible for the **reasoning mind** <term>dianoia: the soul's ability to process logic and reach conclusions step-by-step</term> to reason out the universal from physical occurrences, even if this does not happen in all cases. However, **scientific knowledge** <term>epistemonike gnosis: certain, demonstrated knowledge rather than mere opinion</term> does not view the nature of things in this way for itself. 

Rather, because knowledge is submerged within us—just as some neighbors did not go unnoticed—it is like a **spark hidden in the ashes**. When someone comes along and digs through the ashes for a little fire, the spark immediately flashes out. The one who dug did not create the spark, but only removed the obstacle that was in its way. 

In this same manner, **opinion** <term>doxa: a belief or judgment formed about the sensory world</term>, when stimulated by **sense perception** <term>aisthesis: the data we receive through our eyes, ears, and other senses</term>, brings forward the **thought** <term>noema: an internal concept or object of thought</term> that was already within it. For they say that teachers do not instill knowledge in us from the outside, but rather reveal the knowledge that is already ours and was, as it were, hidden. 

For if these internal thoughts were not the underlying causes of our understanding, why would we pass judgment whenever someone speaks contrary to the nature of things? When <unclear>two people</unclear> are discussing the **soul** <note>original: *psyche*</note>, we are not <unclear>deceived</unclear>, and we refute the speaker if he is not speaking in harmony with the nature of things. Perhaps in this way we posit and say that the soul does not only speak the truth by chance; rather, by comparing what is said with the truths that lie within it, we can say it speaks the truth. This would be impossible if the knowledge of things were not already present within us.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s divisions. Having previously touched upon the "driven" parts (anger and desire) as responses to harm or lack, the text now transitions into the "practical" powers of the rational soul—will and choice—and concludes by defining the lowest level of life: the vegetative soul shared by all living things, including plants.</meta>

...[mortal], [He] gave us **spiritedness** <term>thymos: the seat of anger and courage</term> and **desire** <gloss>for the purpose of</gloss> so that we might ward off those things that harm us, and replenish those things that waste away <note>The author refers to the biological need to replace nutrients lost through bodily "outflow" or decay</note>. These, then, are the cognitive powers of the rational faculties, as they have been divided.

But there are also practical powers, which are **will** <term>boulesis: the rational desire for what is good in itself</term> and **choice** <term>proairesis: the power of deliberate, moral selection between alternatives</term>. **Will** is directed only toward the good; but **choice** is directed toward both [good and evil]. Furthermore, **will** belongs to the rational soul in its own essence, while **choice** belongs to the soul when it is intertwined with **irrationality** <note>original: alogia; the non-reasoning part of the soul that governs impulses and physical needs</note>.

For when the soul was outside the realm of **generation** <term>genesis: the physical world of birth, change, and decay</term>, it acted according to **will** alone, for it existed only within the Good. But when it enters into generation, because the irrational powers are intertwined with it through an innate cause, it then possesses **choice** through the subversion of irrationality. This is because it at one time aligns with irrationality and at another time with the **intellect** <note>original: nous</note>, choosing this thing over that.

These, then, are the psychological powers of the soul. In addition to these are those called the **vegetative** powers. 

<margin>3 vegetative powers</margin> These are three: the **nutritive**, the **augmentative** <note>the power of growth</note>, and the **generative**. They are called "vegetative" because these alone are observed in plants. For they are nourished when watered and fertilized, they grow, and they generate things similar to themselves; for a vine comes from a vine, and an olive from an olive.

To speak by way of summary: both animals and plants are **ensouled** <term>empsycha: literally "having soul," used to describe any living thing</term>. And just as we have enumerated all the psychological powers—likewise <gloss>not</gloss>—treating the irrational powers as belonging to animals, and the vegetative powers as belonging to **ensouled** beings in general. For we say that even plants have a soul; for things that grow, are nourished, and generate their own kind are ensouled. Indeed, they too are called "living," even if they die.

It also defines the 'vegetative soul'—the basic biological functions of nutrition, growth, and reproduction shared by plants, animals, and humans.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s functions. Life and death are the presence and absence of the soul <unclear>it seems</unclear>. Therefore, whatever things possess the higher forms of life certainly also possess the lower forms. To be sure, that which is good no longer participates in the higher if it does not participate in the lower; again, that in which God participates, these include hearing and the rest. And whatever belongs to hearing, these belong to nature and knowledge, though not necessarily to God [in the same way]. As for certainty: to be sure, there are certain parts of us that participate [in life], such as the bones. Nor is it possible to participate in the higher without participating in the lesser. 

But this does not mean the higher beings require the lower in order to exist; rather, on the contrary, the body cannot participate in the higher things without first partaking in the lower. For the body cannot partake in **reason** <note>original: logos</note> without first partaking in **nature** <term>physis: here referring to the basic biological or vegetative power</term>; nor can it partake in the **rational soul** without partaking in both of these.

Since it is necessary that none of the **forms** <term>eidos: the eternal "blueprints" or species of things</term> perish, so that the Whole <note>The universe or the "All"</note> does not fail—for the world is a **fullness** <term>pleroma: a state of being completely filled or whole</term> of these forms—and since it was impossible for all individual things to remain the same in **number** <note>original: arithmos; meaning that individuals cannot live forever as the same numerical unit</note>, all things become perishable, yet they participate in **eternity** <term>aidiotes: everlasting existence</term> as much as they are able. Since everything indeed desires the primal eternity of its own nature and each participates in it according to its own measure, for this reason, since individuals cannot be eternal in number, each participates in eternity by **begetting** another like itself. What is the account regarding the **affections** <note>original: "pathe"; these are the passions, emotions, or "things that happen" to the soul, such as anger or fear</note>? Whether they are not separable from matter, or not separable at all. The **natural philosopher** <note>original: "physikos"; a scientist of nature</note> deals with all things that are the functions and affections of such a body and such matter. But for those things that are not of this kind, another scholar handles them; yet a specific craft might also deal with some, if it so happens, such as that of carpenters or doctors. Regarding those things that are not separable from the body, yet are not viewed as affections of a specific body, but rather through **abstraction**, the **mathematician** <note>original: "mathematikos"</note> investigates these. But insofar as things are considered as separated from matter entirely, the **first philosopher** <note>original: "protos philosophos"; what we today call a "metaphysician"</note> deals with them.

But we must return to where our argument began. We were saying, then, that the **affections of the soul** are not separable from the physical matter of animals, insofar as such things exist—namely **anger and fear**—and they are not like a mathematical **line or a plane**. 

As we are examining the soul, it is necessary to simultaneously work through the difficulties about which one must be puzzled. -> **The Soul as the Principle of Motion** <-

The soul seems to be distinguished by two features especially: **motion** and **sensation**.

According to **Plato** <note>Specifically referring to the *Timaeus*, where Plato describes the world-soul as being composed of the same elements as the universe</note>; for they say that like is known by like. Those, therefore, who say there is only one cause and one element, also posit that the soul is one—such as fire or air. But those who say there are several principles also make the soul several. 

**Anaxagoras** <note>A 5th-century BCE philosopher who introduced the concept of Mind (Nous) as an ordering force</note> alone says that the **Mind** <term>nous: the intellect or capacity for rational thought</term> is "impassive" <note>original: "apathē," meaning it cannot be affected or changed by external things</note>, and that it has nothing in common with anything else. However, all those who create oppositions among the principles also constitute the soul out of these opposites. Others choose one of the opposites—such as heat or cold, or something of that sort. For this reason, they also follow the etymology of the names: those who call it heat argue that the soul <note>original: "psuchē"</note> is named from "to boil" <note>original: "zein"</note> and "to live" <note>original: "zēn"</note>. <meta>This page continues Aristotle's *De Anima* (On the Soul). The previous page concluded the discussion of early elemental theories of the soul (like those of Plato, Empedocles, and Anaxagoras). This page begins Book I, Chapter 3, where Aristotle starts his critical examination of the theory that the soul is "that which moves itself."</meta>

->+<-

<margin>
+ On the Soul
</margin>

<gloss>body &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; certain things are participated in &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; it is moved &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; soul</gloss>

Furthermore, we must first consider **motion**. For perhaps it is not only false that the soul's **essence** <term>ousia: the fundamental nature or substance of a thing</term> is as those say who claim the soul is that which moves itself or is capable of moving, but it may be one of the things that is simply impossible: for motion to belong to the soul at all. It has been stated previously <note>original: "πρότερον εἴρηται"; Aristotle refers to his *Physics*, where he argues that the "First Mover" must be unmoved</note> that it is not necessary for that which moves something to be moved itself. Everything that moves does so in two ways: it is moved either **through another** or **by itself**. 

We say things move "through another" when they move because they are inside something else that is moving—for example, **sailors** <note>Aristotle uses the famous "sailor on a ship" analogy to distinguish between "accidental" motion (moving because your container moves) and "essential" motion (moving your own limbs)</note>. They do not move in the same way the ship does; for the ship moves **by itself**, while the sailors move by being inside that which is moving. This is clear if we look at the parts of the body. Walking is the "proper motion" of the feet, and thus the motion of men; however, this motion does not belong to the sailors at that time. 

Since "to be moved" is spoken of in these two ways, we are now examining the soul to see if it moves "by itself" and participates in motion. There are **four kinds of motion**: **locomotion** <term>phora: movement from place to place</term>, **alteration** <term>alloiōsis: qualitative change, like turning from cold to hot</term>, **decay**, and **growth**. If the soul moves, it must move with one of these, or several, or all of them. But if it moves not by accident, but by its very nature...

...if motion belongs to it. And if this is so, it also occupies a **place** <term>topos: a specific location or spatial position in the physical world</term>. All the types of motion we have discussed follow logically: if the **essence** <term>ousia: the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing</term> of the soul is to move itself, then being moved <gloss>exists</gloss> is not an "accidental" property for it. By "accidental," we mean the way a color like **whiteness** or a measurement like **three cubits long** is moved. For these also move, but only by accident <gloss>in the body</gloss>; for the body to which they belong is what moves, and because of this <gloss>at</gloss> they do not have a place of their own. But the soul will have a place, if indeed it participates in motion by nature. <gloss>And what he said: it moves also by nature</gloss> Furthermore, if it moves by nature, it could also be moved by **force** <term>bia: unnatural or external compulsion, often translated as "violent" motion</term>; and if it can be moved by force, it can also be moved by nature. The same holds true regarding **rest** <term>eremia: the state of being at a standstill</term>. For wherever a thing moves naturally, it also rests there naturally;

<meta>This page continues Aristotle's inquiry into whether the soul moves. On the previous page, he established that if the soul moves naturally, it must have a physical location and be subject to the laws of motion and rest. Here, he explores the logical absurdities that arise if we assume the soul moves in the same way bodies do, specifically the idea that it could exit and re-enter a body, or that it could be "displaced" from its own nature.</meta>

<margin>
6. This and itself
<image-desc>A small crescent-shaped diagram with textual labels: "nature," "motion," "according to the," and "body."</image-desc>

...it is reasonable that the soul initiates motions in the same way that it is itself moved. And if
this is so, it is also true to say that the soul's revolution <note>original: "strephin"</note>—that is, that it 
moves the body—is both accidental <term>symbebekos: a property that is not essential to a thing's nature, like a person's hair color</term> and according to its form. The body
<margin>

On the Soul
<note>original Latin: "Lib I de anim"</note>

moves by locomotion <term>phora: spatial movement from one place to another</term>, so the soul would also change its position according to the 
body, either moving as a whole or shifting part by part. And if this is possible, 
it would also be possible for the soul to leave the body and enter it
<margin>
One might say that the soul itself is moved especially by sensible objects <note>i.e., things perceived by the senses like sight or sound</note>.
</margin>
once again. But from this, it would follow that dead animals could rise again. 
As for accidental motion, even if the soul were moved by something else, 
the animal would be pushed by force <term>bia: motion against a thing's natural inclination</term>. 
But that which has "self-motion" in its **essence** <term>ousia: the core being or definition of a thing</term> 
should not be moved by another, except perhaps by accident. 
Just as the "good in itself" <note>a philosophical concept of something that is fundamentally good, not just good for a specific purpose</note> exists for its own sake, 
while another thing exists for the sake of something else. 
Now, one might say that the soul is moved 
especially by sensible objects, if indeed it moves at all. 
But if the soul moves itself, it would also be moved by itself. 
So, if every motion is a **displacement** <term>ekstasis: literally "standing out of" or a change from a previous state</term> of the thing moved 
insofar as it is moved, then the soul would also be "displaced" from its own essence.

<meta>This page continues Aristotle's critique of earlier philosophers' theories of the soul. On the previous page, he argued that if the soul moves, it must do so either essentially or accidentally. Here, he examines specific mechanical theories of the soul's movement—specifically those of Democritus and Plato’s Timaeus—arguing that they fail to account for the role of the will and intellect.</meta>

->+<-

<margin>
Concerning the motions of the soul

<margin>

# On Harmony

<margin>
On harmony
</margin>

There is another theory handed down to us that is no less persuasive than those already mentioned. To many, it seems the most plausible <note>original: "logos de hōs peri autōn" – an account concerning these things</note> among the views expressed, and it has even been defended in public discussions. For some say the soul is a certain kind of **harmony**. They argue that harmony is a **mixture** <term>krasis: a blending of qualities like hot and cold</term> and a **composition** of <gloss>opposites</gloss> opposites, and that the body itself is composed of <gloss>the</gloss> <gloss>opposites or rather opposites but the opposites equal in number the opposites or rather the opposites</gloss> opposites.

However, while a harmony is a certain **ratio** <term>logos: here meaning a mathematical proportion or relationship</term> of things that have been mixed, or a composition, it is impossible for the soul to be either of these. Furthermore, <gloss>the power to move</gloss> the capacity to produce motion is not a property of harmony; yet nearly everyone, one might say, attributes this especially to the soul. It is more fitting to speak of harmony in relation to **health**, and generally in terms of the physical virtues of the body,

<margin>
It is clear if one should attempt to attribute the passions of the soul to a certain harmony.
</margin>

rather than in relation to the soul. This becomes most evident if one tries to attribute the passions <note>original: "pathe" – the emotions, sufferings, or passive states of the soul</note> and functions of the soul to a specific harmony; for it is difficult to make them fit. 

Furthermore, we use the term "harmony" with two different meanings in mind. Most strictly, it refers to the arrangement of magnitudes <note>physical objects with size and extension</note> in things that possess motion and position, when they are so fitted together that they do not admit anything of the same kind into the gaps. From this, the term is also applied to the **ratio** of things that are mixed together. In neither of these senses is it reasonable to call the soul a harmony. Moreover, the **composition** of the parts of the body is very easy to examine...

...and of the solid parts, and in many ways. Of what, then, is it the <gloss>ratio</gloss> <note>original: *logos*—meaning a mathematical proportion</note>?

<margin>For what does he say being "harmony" itself signifies? Either being accidental, or double, or one-and-a-half?</margin>

One might demand an answer to this even from **Empedocles** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that all matter is composed of four elements—earth, air, fire, and water—joined by Love and separated by Strife.</note>; for he says that each of the parts—<gloss>flesh, etc.</gloss>—is a certain ratio. Is the soul, then, the ratio <gloss>beyond chance</gloss>, or is it rather something else existing in the limbs? 

Furthermore, is **Love** <note>original: *philia*—the cosmic force of attraction in Empedocles' system</note> the cause of any random mixture, or only of the one according to the ratio? And is Love itself the ratio, or is it something else besides the ratio? These questions indeed involve such difficulties. But the soul would seem to be something other than the mixture. For if being <gloss>harmony</gloss> <gloss>ratio</gloss> flesh is destroyed, then so too are the other parts of the animal. In addition, if each of the parts has a soul <gloss>harmony</gloss>—unless the soul itself is the ratio of the mixture.

<summary>This page contains Aristotle's refutation of the theory that the soul is a "self-moving number," arguing that mathematical units (monads) cannot logically possess movement or position in the way a soul does. It also distinguishes the "intellect" (nous) as a divine, impassive element that survives the death of the physical body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Aristotle’s critique of the "soul as a self-moving number" theory, specifically addressing the logical inconsistencies that arise when one tries to explain human emotions and perceptions using mathematical units. It transitions from a critique of movement-based theories to a critique of elemental theories (the idea that the soul is made of physical elements like fire or air).</meta>

In either case, it is necessary for the living creature to move because these units move. For those who have intertwined movement and number into the same definition, these consequences follow, along with many other such difficulties. Not only is it impossible for such a thing to be the definition of the soul, but it cannot even be its accidental property <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accidental property" is a quality that isn't essential to what a thing is, like being musical is to a human</note>. <meta>This page continues the transition into Aristotle’s critique of the materialist view of the soul—specifically the idea that the soul is composed of the same physical elements (earth, air, fire, water) as the world it perceives. Aristotle is now examining the principle of "like knows like," famously championed by the philosopher-poet Empedocles.</meta>

<margin>
By the same thing, like knows like; the soul knows composite things <note>A "composite" is any complex thing made of multiple parts, like a physical body</note>. Indeed, to know like by like, as <unclear>Empedocles</unclear> says, the soul of each thing knows the composites that are made from those elements.
</margin>

<image-desc>
A diagram in the left margin consisting of two sets of crescent-shaped brackets used to organize philosophical and poetic concepts. The upper diagram lists the elements (earth, water, air, fire, love, strife) and states they are known by the soul. The lower diagram questions how complex entities like God, man, flesh, and bone are known, suggesting they are known through logic and composition.
</image-desc>

<margin>
"For with earth we see earth, with water, water, with air, divine air, and with fire, consuming fire; with Love, Love, and with Strife, baneful Strife" <note>This is a famous fragment from Empedocles’ poem "On Nature," expressing the idea that we can only perceive the universe because we are made of the same materials</note>. For the soul knows these things.
</margin>

<margin>
What will God be, or man, or flesh, or bone, or whatever else among the composites? Such things will exist by proportion and composition. How does the soul know these? Or does it not know them in this way?
</margin>

<margin>
As the poet says <note>Empedocles</note>, because the elements are in the soul—such as earth, water, and the rest—in this way he also places knowledge within the soul.
</margin>

They propose that like is known by like, as if they were placing the physical things themselves inside the soul. But these elements are not the only things that exist. There are many other things—perhaps even infinite in number—that are formed from them. Let it be granted that the soul knows and perceives each of the elements from which things are made. But the whole—by what will the soul recognize or perceive it? For example, what is God, or man, or flesh, or bone? The same question applies to any other composite thing. For the elements do not form these things by just being combined in any random way; rather, they exist according to a certain <term>proportion; original: logos; here referring to the specific ratio or structural formula of a thing</term> and composition, just as Empedocles says <gloss>in the first book of his work "On Nature"</gloss> regarding bone:

> And the kindly earth <note>original: chthon</note> in its broad-chested melting-pots
> received two parts of the eight shares,
> while four were from Hephaestus <note>a poetic name for fire</note>. And the white bones
> were born.

There is no benefit, then, in the elements being present in the soul, unless the proportions and the composition are also present. For while each element in the soul would recognize its like in the world, the soul would recognize nothing of a "bone" or a "man" unless those specific structures were also inside it. It should not even be necessary to say that this is impossible. For who would even ask whether a stone or a man is literally present inside the soul? The same logic applies to the "Good" and the "Not-Good," and in the same way to all other things.

<summary>Aristotle critiques Empedocles’ theory that the soul knows the world because it is made of the same elements, arguing that knowing a "bone" requires the soul to contain the specific ratio of elements, not just the elements themselves.</summary>
<keywords>Empedocles, Aristotle, elements, proportion, bone, like knows like, psychology, philosophy of mind, composition</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Aristotle’s critique of the materialist view of the soul. In the previous section, we saw the famous idea from the philosopher Empedocles that "like knows like"—that we perceive the physical world (earth, air, fire, water) because our own souls are made of those very same elements. Here, Aristotle applies his own logical system, the "Categories," to show the flaws in this thinking.</meta>

+

+ Since "being" <term>being (τὸ ὄν): the basic concept of existence or what it means for something to "be"</term> is spoken of in many ways, it signifies in one sense a "this" <term>substance (τόδε τι): a specific, individual thing like a person or a stone</term>, in another a quantity, or a quality, or any other of the divided categories. We must ask whether the soul <note>original: "ψυχή" (psychē)</note> is composed of all of these or not. It does not seem that the elements are everything. From which, as many things as are substances, are composed of these only. How then does the soul know each of the perceptible things? Or do some say there are elements and principles unique to each genus <term>genus: a class or group of things</term>, from which the soul is composed? If so, the soul will therefore be both a quantity and a quality. But this is impossible—that a substance could be made from the elements of quantity and yet not itself be a quantity. To those who say the soul is made of all things, these and other such absurdities follow.
<gloss>absurdities when they occur so that even the sensory things <unclear>...</unclear></gloss>
And it is absurd to say that while "like" is unaffected by "like," yet like perceives like, and like knows like by means of like. Yet they define the act of perceiving as being affected by something and being moved.
<gloss>the difficulties themselves belong to these theories</gloss>
The same applies to thinking and knowing. Many are the problems and difficulties held by those who speak just as Empedocles does: that each thing is recognized by the bodily elements, and according to that which is like...
<gloss>like</gloss>

<summary>Aristotle critiques the theory that the soul is composed of physical elements, arguing that this would force the soul to also be a physical quantity or quality, which is logically impossible. He specifically challenges Empedocles' "like knows like" principle by pointing out that perception is a process of being changed or affected, which should not happen between two identical things.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Aristotle's critique of earlier theories of the soul. ...of the truth. But if it is necessary to make the soul out of the elements, there is no need to make it out of all of them. One part of an **opposition** <note>original: "ἐναντιώσεως" (enantiōseōs). Aristotle refers to pairs of opposites, like hot and cold or straight and curved.</note> is sufficient to judge both itself and its opposite. For by means of the straight, we recognize both the straight itself and the curved; for the **ruler** <note>original: "κανών" (kanōn). A straight-edge or measuring rod used as a standard for judgment.</note> is the judge of both, whereas the curved is a judge of neither itself nor the straight.

And some say that the soul is mixed into the whole universe; which is perhaps why Thales thought that **"all things are full of gods."** <note>Thales of Miletus (6th century BCE) is considered the first Western philosopher. This famous phrase suggests that a life-force or divinity permeates all physical matter.</note>

<margin>Difficulty <note>original: "ἀπορία" (aporia). A philosophical puzzle or a "dead end" that requires a solution.</note></margin>
This view, however, presents certain difficulties. For what cause is it that the soul, when it exists in the air or in the fire, does not produce a **living being** <note>original: "ζῷον" (zōon). Usually translated as "animal," but refers generally to any living thing with a soul.</note>, yet it does so when in mixtures of the elements—and this despite the soul appearing to be of a higher quality when it exists in these [pure elements]? One might also inquire as to the reason why the soul in the air is "better" and more immortal than the soul found in living beings.

The result in both cases is absurd and irrational. For to call fire or air a "living being" is among the more irrational claims. Yet, not to call them living beings when a soul is present in them is also absurd. They seem to assume that the soul is in these elements because the whole is **of the same nature** as its parts; so it is necessary for them...

<meta>This page continues Aristotle's investigation into whether the soul is a single, unified entity or a collection of parts. # +

...to say the soul is of the same kind as its parts. In which case --- 
but one must take into account what happens in animals. For some 
<gloss>or being divided</gloss>
animals, when torn apart, become similar in form <note>Aristotle is likely referring to creatures like flatworms or certain insects that continue to move or live even after being cut into pieces.</note>.
But if the soul is composed of unlike parts <note>original: "ἀνομοιομερῆ" (anomoiomerē). This refers to a whole made of different types of components, like a body made of hands, eyes, and lungs.</note>, it will not possess any unity. 
And if it has no unity, then it must be that either the parts of the universe are made of like parts <note>original: "ὁμοιομερῆ" (homoiomerē). Substances that are uniform throughout, where every part is the same as the whole, like water or gold.</note>, or that no soul exists at all in the whole part of the universe.

It is certainly not the body; for the opposite seems rather to be the case—that the soul holds the body together. Indeed, once the soul has departed, the body evaporates and decays. If, then, some other thing <gloss>some one thing</gloss> makes the soul one, that thing would most truly be the soul. But then it will be necessary to inquire again into that thing: whether it is one or made of many parts. For if it is one, why not immediately say that the soul itself is one?
