<meta>This page follows the discussion where Aristotle established that substance can be understood as matter, form, or a composite. He is now refining the definition of the soul as the "form" or "actuality" of a living body, concluding the transition from a general to a specific definition.</meta>

<image-desc>In the left margin, a faint geometric diagram of a triangle is visible, likely bleed-through from the preceding leaf or a very lightly drawn marginal note. It contains small characters at its vertices, likely labeling them as alpha (α), beta (β), and gamma (γ).</image-desc>

...to speak: the **soul** is the **first actuality** <term>entelecheia: the state of a thing being fully realized or functional, like the transition from having a skill to actually using it</term> of a natural, organized body. Therefore, there is no need to inquire whether the soul and the body are one, just as we do not ask if the wax and the shape impressed upon it are one, or generally, whether the matter of a thing and that of which it is the matter are one. For although "one" and "being" are used in many ways, the primary sense is that of **actuality** <note>original: "entelecheia"</note>. 

We have now stated in general terms what the soul is: it is **substance** <note>original: "ousia"</note> in the sense of the definition <term>logos: the essential formula or "account" of what a thing is</term>. This is the very essence <term>to ti ēn einai: literally "the what it was to be," meaning the core identity that makes a thing what it is</term> of a body of a certain kind—<gloss>natural and organic</gloss>.

Consider this: if an instrument, such as an axe, were a natural body, then "axe-ness" would be its substance, and this would be its soul. If this were taken away, it would no longer be an axe, except in name only <note>original: "homōnymōs"</note>; as it is, it remains an axe. But the soul is not the essence and definition of an object like that, but rather of a natural body of a specific kind—one that has the principle of motion and rest within itself.

We must also apply what has been said to the individual parts of the body. <gloss>For if the eye were a living creature, sight would be its soul; for this is the substance of the eye in the sense of its definition.</gloss> For if the eye were a living creature, **sight** would be its **soul**; for this is the **substance** of the eye in accordance with its **definition**. The eye itself is the matter <note>original: "hylē"</note> of sight. If sight is lost, the eye is no longer an eye, except in name—just like an eye made of stone or one in a painting. What we have said about the part, we must now apply to the whole living body.

<summary>Aristotle defines the soul as the "first actuality" of a natural body and uses the analogy of an axe and an eye to show that the soul is to the body what sight is to the eye—its essential function and purpose.</summary>

...ific kind of living body. Just as a part relates to a part, the whole of **sensation** <term>aisthēsis: the capacity for perception through the senses</term> relates to the entire sensing body, insofar as it is such a body. Now, it is not the body that has lost its soul that is **potentially** <term>dynamis: the power or capacity to do something, as opposed to its actual performance</term> alive, but rather the one that possesses it. The seed and the fruit are also the body in **potentiality**. 

Therefore, just as cutting is to the axe and seeing is to the eye, so the state of **waking** is **actuality** <note>original: "entelecheia"</note>; but the soul is like sight or the power of the tool itself. The body is merely that which exists in potentiality. But just as an eye is the combination of the pupil and the sight, so the soul and the body together constitute the **living being**.

It is clear, then, that the **soul** is not separable from the body—or at least certain parts of it are not, if the soul is by nature divisible into parts. For the **actuality** of some parts of the soul belongs to the body parts themselves. However, nothing prevents some other parts of the soul from being separable, because they are not the actualities of any physical body. Furthermore, it is still unclear whether the soul is the **actuality** of the body in the same way that a **pilot is to a ship** <note>This is a famous Aristotelian problem: if the soul is the "form" of the body, it shouldn't be separable, yet a pilot can step off a boat. But since clarity and a more rational understanding arise from things that are obscure <gloss>though more obvious to us</gloss> yet clearer <gloss>or better known by nature</gloss>, we must try once more to...

### The Nutritive and Generative Soul

Now that the causes have been defined, we must speak about nourishment and reproduction, <note>Aristotle argues that to understand a "power" (like digestion), one must first look at the "act" (eating) and the "object" (food).</note> for the "soul of the being" and "where it is." Consequently, we must first speak about nourishment and reproduction <gloss>the generative power</gloss> more fully.

The **nutritive soul** belongs to all other [living things]. It is the first and most common power of the soul, through which life belongs to all. Its functions are to reproduce and to use nourishment. <gloss>To reproduce something like itself</gloss> is for each individual <gloss>among living things</gloss>, <gloss>those which are complete</gloss> <gloss>and</gloss> <gloss>not defects</gloss> <margin>aside from</margin> or those which have spontaneous generation, <note>Ancient Greeks believed some small creatures, like flies or worms, could emerge "spontaneously" from decaying matter rather than from parents.</note> to produce another like itself: an animal produces an animal, a plant produces a plant. They do this so that they may partake in the **eternal** and the **divine** as much as they are able, for all things desire that. For the sake of that [the divine], they do whatever they do according to nature. 

The phrase "for the sake of which" <note>original: *to d'hou heneka* — a technical term for the 'Final Cause' or the purpose of an action.</note> has two meanings: the purpose *for which* a thing is done, and the beneficiary *for whom* it is done. Since, therefore, it is impossible for [perishables] to share in the eternal and the divine through continuity—because no perishable thing can remain exactly the same and **one in number** <note>Meaning: a single individual cannot live forever.</note> —each shares in it in the way it is able. Some share more, some less. It remains not as itself, but as something *like* itself; not one in number, but **one in form** <term>eidos: the species or "kind" of thing, which survives even when the individual dies</term>. <insert>According to</insert> this, the seed of animals is their instrument. 

The **soul** is the cause and principle <term>archē: the starting point or fundamental origin</term> of the living body. These things...

That it is the cause as **essence** is clear. However, there is a difference: the things that trigger the **activity** <term>activity: "energeia," the state of being "at work" or in action</term> are outside the subject—specifically, the visible, the audible, and the rest of the objects of sense. 

The reason for this is that actual perception is of **particulars** <note>original: "kath' hekaston"; specific, individual things like "this red apple"</note>, whereas knowledge is of **universals** <note>original: "katholou"; general concepts or categories like "redness" or "fruit"</note>. These universals are, in a sense, in the **soul** <term>soul: "psyche," the animating principle or mind</term> itself. 

Therefore, thinking is within a person's own power whenever they wish to do so. But perceiving is not within their power in the same way, for it is necessary that the object of sense be physically present. This is also the case with the sciences that deal with sensible things, and for the same reason: because sensible things are particulars and exist outside the mind.

<meta>This page continues Aristotle’s investigation into the physics of sound. <margin>+ On voice.</margin>

This follows the same logic as what we said regarding voiceless sounds: a high pitch <note>original: "oxu," meaning sharp or pointed</note> moves the sense in a certain way, while a low pitch <note>original: "amblu," meaning blunt or dull</note> pushes the sense, as it were, because of how it moves. The former moves in a short time, while the latter moves in a long time; consequently, the one turns out to be fast and the other slow. But since every sound is produced by something striking something else within a medium, and this medium is air, it is logical that only those creatures that breathe in air would have a voice. In these creatures, nature uses the breath for two functions, just as it uses the tongue for both tasting 
<gloss>But this [speech] is for the sake of well-being.</gloss>

<meta>This page continues Aristotle’s biological and psychological analysis of the voice. <gloss>because the soul moves the air, and through this, life is maintained;</gloss>
As for interpretation <note>original: "hermēneia" — here referring to the vocal expression of thought</note>, it exists for the sake of well-being. Thus, the breath <note>term: "pneuma" — the vital breath or spirit that carries life-heat</note> is necessary in relation to the heat of the internal parts; the reason for this will be discussed elsewhere <gloss>that is, in the treatise On the Generation of Animals</gloss> <note>While the gloss identifies the work as "On the Generation of Animals," Aristotle typically treats respiration in "On Respiration" or "Parts of Animals."</note> and in relation to the voice, so that well-being may exist. The organ used for respiration is the pharynx <note>original: "pharunx" — here referring broadly to the throat and windpipe area</note>. And the part for the sake of which this exists is the lung. 

<margin>
Land animals especially use the lung; for not every animal requires the cooling of the lung and the lung itself.
</margin>
By means of this part, land animals possess more heat than all other creatures. They require respiration <gloss>but not every animal; for example, insects do not; but only those having a lung; and of these, those having more heat;</gloss>, just as the heart is the primary place of heat. 

<margin>
But then how does the heart require cooling, such that the heart is also a part involved?
</margin>
On this account, it is necessary for the inhaled air to enter within. Thus, the impact of the inhaled air—driven by the soul residing in these parts against what is called the windpipe <note>term: "artēria" — in ancient Greek biology, this term refers to the trachea or "rough artery," through which air passes</note>—is the voice. For as we said, not every noise made by an animal is a voice. It is possible, for instance, to make a noise with the tongue, or as those who cough do. 

<margin>
Therefore the voice is not located simply in the windpipe of the lung, but is found where the breath is in excess; yet it is not the animal itself that moves [the air] nor the breath outside; for not every animal has a voice. In those that do have a voice, three factors are present, but the heart is the part that governs the breath, as has been said. The breath striking against the windpipe is the air within the windpipe; it strikes it; for the striking is against the windpipe itself. Thus, as the windpipe is vibrated by the air or the breath, the voice is produced.

# The Sense of Taste and the Nature of Perception

...the cause. <meta>This page continues Aristotle's analysis of the senses from his treatise On the Soul. Having established that taste requires moisture and direct contact, he now compares the "tastable" to the "visible," explaining how the organ of taste—the tongue—must be prepared to receive flavors.</meta>

-> + <-

Just as in the case of sight there is the visible and the invisible <gloss>invisible</gloss>, and that which is invisible because it is seen poorly—much like the "invisible" <gloss>or that which is not</gloss> and the fiery <note>original: "katapyrion"—referring to something so intensely bright or "fiery" that it overcomes the eyes and cannot be seen properly</note>. In the same way, taste is concerned with both the tastable and the untastable. The "untastable" refers to that which has either a very small or a poor flavor <note>term: "chymos" — often translated as "juice" or "flavor," the quality of a substance that is perceived by the tongue</note>, or that which is destructive to the sense of taste. 

It seems that the starting point is the "drinkable" and the "undrinkable." For both are perceived by a kind of taste; however, one is poor and destructive to the sense, while the other is according to nature. The drinkable is a quality common to both touch and taste. Since the tastable object is liquid, it is necessary that its sense organ <note>term: "aistheterion" — the physical part of the body, like the tongue, that receives sensory input</note> be neither actually liquid itself, nor incapable of being moistened. For the sense of taste is affected by the tastable object insofar as it is tastable. 

It is necessary, then, that the organ of taste—which is capable of being moistened while preserving its own nature, yet is not itself liquid—be moistened. Evidence for this is the fact that the tongue does not perceive flavor when it is either completely parched or excessively moist. In the latter case, the sensation becomes merely the touch of the initial liquid already present. This is similar to when someone has first tasted a strong flavor and then tries to taste something else. It is also why everything seems bitter to those who are sick, because they perceive things through a tongue that is already full of such bitter moisture. As for the types of flavors, they follow a pattern like that of colors...

<margin>
The "undrinkable" has two meanings. One is absolute, as having no flavor at all, just as the "invisible" has no color. The other is the "untastable," or that which has no taste. That which has a poor flavor, or even a partially bad one, is also destructive to the sense of taste. This is also how the term "usage" <note>The writer likely refers to how we commonly name things based on how we use or experience them</note> was applied.
</margin>

<summary>Aristotle explains that taste requires the tongue to be potentially moist but not saturated, comparing the "untastable" to things that are "invisible" due to lack of color or excessive brightness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Aristotle's investigation into the mechanics of touch. The previous page established that flesh is likely a medium of sensation rather than the organ itself, arguing that a living body cannot be made of a single element. This page extends that logic by comparing touch to sight and hearing, suggesting that all senses require a medium, even if that medium is so close (like skin) that we fail to notice it.</meta>

...another in water; it is the same way in the air. For the air stands in the same relation to the things in it as water does to the things in
<gloss>everything in the air and everything in the water</gloss> water. This escapes our notice even more, just as it does with animals living in air or water, if they touch one thing through another. Is **perception** <term>aisthesis — sensory awareness</term> of all things then similar, or does it happen differently for different things, as it is currently thought? While **taste** <term>geusis</term> and **touch** <term>haphe</term> are believed to be senses that function by direct contact, this is actually not the case for them. Rather, we perceive even the hard and the soft through something else, just as we do with sound, the visible, and the fragrant. The difference is that some are perceived from a distance, and others from close by. For this reason it escapes our notice; for we actually perceive all things through a **medium** <note>original: "dia tou mesou" — the intervening material like air, water, or flesh</note>. But in these specific cases, it is hidden. Yet, as we said before, even if we were to perceive all tangible things through a membrane
<margin>+ the membrane: the skin: or also the covering <note>original: "chiton" — literally a tunic or outer layer</note>.</margin>
and it went unnoticed that it separates us, we would be in the same situation as we are now in the water and the air. But the tangible differs from the visible and the audible because we perceive those other things because the intervening medium acts upon us...

For in this way, the same thing happens as with the other senses: when objects are placed directly upon the sense organ, it does not perceive; but when they are placed upon the flesh, it does perceive. Therefore, the **medium** <note>original: "to metaxy" — the "in-between" material</note> of the tactile sense is the flesh. Yet, they act together simultaneously.

<gloss>The sensing element is the **mean** <note>original: "μέσον" (meson) – a middle or neutral point</note> between the opposites found in the objects of sense. This mean judges the sensory objects, for the middle state is capable of judgment.</gloss>

<margin>He showed that the middle state is capable of judging. This middle state exists for all sensible objects. He says it acts in relation to the extremes in the senses.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the sensory organs. Having established that touch requires a neutral state to perceive extremes, Aristotle now broadens his scope to a general definition of all sensation. He explains that sensation is not the physical absorption of an object, but the reception of its "form" alone, much like an impression in wax.</meta>

->+<-

<margin>
First, he mentioned the primary sense organ, in which the sensory power resides: namely, the underlying subject of the soul is the first sense organ—first in sensation by the contribution within it of the sense organ toward the instrument, as the forms and species. For it is not through an internal surrender that the sensory power of the soul acts, but it is sent out through these existing things toward that object.
</margin>

<margin>
He explains the nature of the sensory power, and not just the sense organ; and if it were the organ, how would he say, for example, that it receives forms without matter? Sensation [receives them], but not the underlying physical subject; or the spirit <note>original: "πνεύματος" (pneumatos) – here referring to the physiological "pneuma" or breath thought to carry sensory information</note> of the sense organ receives it. This is a sign because the underlying subject does not <unclear>remain</unclear> in a state of transformation, but acts as matter with its own form. Since our sensation is **one** in its form.
</margin>

...matter; for example, the wax receives the impression of the signet ring, but it does not receive the mark in its capacity as iron or gold. Rather, it receives the golden or bronze impression, but not insofar as it is gold or bronze. In the same way, each sense is affected by that which has color, or flavor, or sound; but it is not affected by them as they are defined individually, but insofar as they have a certain quality and according to their **proportion** <note>original: "λόγον" (logon) – here meaning the specific ratio or mathematical balance that defines a sensation</note>. The primary sense organ <term>aisthētērion|the physical body part that senses</term>, in which such a power resides, is indeed the same [as the body], but its "being" is different. For that which perceives must have some magnitude; however, the "being sensory" or "sensation" itself is not a magnitude, but rather a certain proportion and power of that magnitude.

**It is clear** from this why the excesses of sensible objects destroy the sense organs. For if the movement is stronger than the sense organ, the **proportion** <note>original: "logos"</note> is destroyed. This proportion is what sensation was, just as harmony and pitch [are destroyed] when strings are struck too violently. This also explains why plants do not perceive, even though they have a psychic part <note>the "vegetative soul" responsible for growth and nutrition</note> and are affected by tangible things; <gloss>for they are <unclear>also</unclear> affected by them</gloss> for they are cooled and heated. The cause is that they lack a **mean** <term>mesotes|a neutral middle point or balance</term>, and do not possess a principle capable of receiving the forms of sensible objects.

<margin>
For sensation is a certain proportion <unclear>underlying</unclear> a thing; the <unclear>uneven</unclear> and the <unclear>mean</unclear>. The underlying sensory power is a body or a magnitude. The sensory element must be considered not according to magnitude, but according to sensation.
</margin>

<summary>Aristotle defines sensation as the reception of the "form" of an object without its physical "matter," using the analogy of a wax seal. It is clear that seeing and perceiving are not a single, simple thing. For even when we are not seeing <note>Aristotle refers here to seeing in the dark, where the eye still "judges" the absence of light.</note> we judge both darkness and light by our sight, though not in the same way. Furthermore, that which sees is itself, in a sense, colored; for each sensory organ <gloss>the underlying subject</gloss> is receptive to the sensible object without its matter. This is why, even after the sensible objects have gone away, sensations and mental images <term>phantasiai: internal mental pictures or impressions</term> persist within the sensory organs. Now, the activity of the sensible object <gloss>the underlying subject</gloss> and the activity of the sense are one and the same, although their fundamental essence <gloss>in nature and substance</gloss> is not the same. I mean, for example, actual sound and actual hearing. It is possible for someone to have the power of hearing without actually hearing at that moment, and that which has the potential to make a sound does not always make a sound. But when that which is capable of hearing actually exercises that power, and that which is capable of sounding actually makes a sound, then the actual hearing and the <gloss>in the underlying subject</gloss> actual sound occur simultaneously. Of these, one might call <gloss>the sensation</gloss> "hearing," and the other <gloss>the action</gloss> "sounding." If then <gloss>motion, action, and affection</gloss> motion, action, and affection <note>original: "pathos" - the experience of being acted upon.</note> are located in the thing being acted upon, then it is necessary that both the sound and the hearing in their actual state exist within the potential sense-faculty. For the activity of the acting and moving agent takes place within the subject that is being acted upon; for this reason, it is not necessary for the mover itself to be moved.

->to be moved<-

<summary>Aristotle explains that the act of perceiving (like hearing) and the act of being perceived (like a sound) are a single event occurring in the listener. He also notes that sense organs retain "images" of objects even after the objects are gone because they receive the form of the object without its physical matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of sensory perception from Aristotle’s *De Anima*. The previous page concluded by noting that while the sensing organ and the object being sensed (like a sound or a color) have different "essences" or definitions, they share a single, unified "activity" or "event" when perception actually occurs. This page explores how this unified activity is named (or why it lacks a name) and critiques earlier philosophers who argued that objects have no qualities unless they are being observed.</meta>

-> + <-

If, then, this is the activity of the productive agency <term>poietikou: the object that creates a sound or sensation</term> and is a "sounding," and if the activity of the auditory faculty is "hearing" or the "act of hearing"—for hearing is twofold and sound is twofold <note>Aristotle means that both "hearing" and "sound" can refer to a potential (the ability to hear/make sound) or an actuality (the current event of hearing/making sound).</note>—the same principle applies to the other senses and objects of sensation. And just as acting and being acted upon take place in the thing being acted upon, and not in the actor, so too the activity of the sensing faculty and the activity of the object being sensed occur within the sensing faculty. 

But in some cases, these activities have specific names, such as "sounding" and "hearing"; in other cases, one or the other remains nameless. For "seeing" is the name given to the activity of sight, but the activity of color <note>original: "ἡ δὲ τοῦ χρώματος"</note> is nameless. Likewise, "tasting" is the activity of the tasting faculty, but the activity of flavor <note>original: "ἡ δὲ τοῦ χυμοῦ"</note> remains nameless. 

Since the activity of the sensed object and that of the sensing faculty is one and the same—though their fundamental essence is different—it is necessary that hearing and sound, or flavor and taste, and the others likewise, must cease to exist and continue to exist simultaneously. However, this is not necessary for those things spoken of in terms of potentiality <note>A bell has the *potential* to sound even when silent; a person has the *potential* to hear even in a quiet room. These potentials do not need to "perish" together.</note>. 

The earlier natural philosophers <term>physiologoi: the "physicists" or pre-Socratic thinkers who studied nature</term> did not speak correctly on this point, for they believed that nothing was either white or black without sight, nor was there flavor without taste. In one sense, they were speaking correctly <note>They were right that "actual" color requires a viewer, but wrong to suggest that the "potential" for color does not exist independently.</note>.

<summary>Aristotle argues that the "act" of perceiving and the "act" of being perceived are a single event occurring within the observer. He further critiques earlier thinkers by distinguishing between the existence of a quality (like color) as a potentiality versus its existence as an active sensation.</summary>

However, they <note>The earlier "natural philosophers" or Pre-Socratics.</note> were not entirely correct. For we speak of sensation and the sensible object in two ways: some according to potentiality <term>dynamis: the latent capacity to sense or be sensed</term>, and others according to activity <term>energeia: the actualized state of sensing or being sensed</term>. In the case of actualized sensing, the previous statement holds true; but in the other case of potentiality, it does not. Those earlier thinkers spoke in absolute terms about things that are not absolute. 

Since harmony <note>original: "symphonia"</note> is a kind of sound, and sound and hearing are in one sense the same and in another sense not the same, the same follows for harmony. For this reason, since harmony <gloss>destroys</gloss>—and this is <gloss>necessary</gloss>—then hearing must also be a kind of proportion <term>logos: here, a mathematical ratio or structured balance</term>. 

And for this very reason, every excess <gloss>destroys</gloss> the sense—both the high-pitched and the low-pitched sound destroy the hearing. In flavors, the same occurs with sweetness; and in colors, with light that is <gloss>bright</gloss>, or rather excessively bright, or even the murky. In the sense of smell, a strong odor likewise destroys, whether it be sweet or bitter. This happens because the sense is a kind of proportion. For this reason, sensations are pleasant when they are brought into the proportion in a pure and unmixed state—such as the sharp, the sweet, or the salty. They are pleasant then. Generally, however, a mixture is more of a harmony than just the high or the low pitch. In touch, it is the heating <gloss>or</gloss> cooling. The sensation is the proportion; but excesses cause pain or destruction. Each sense, then, is concerned with its underlying sensible object.

Furthermore, perceptions are always true, whereas imaginations are for the most part false. 

Then again, we do not say, when we are actively perceiving an object accurately, "this appears to us as a man"; rather, we say this when we do not perceive it clearly; then [the appearance] is either true or <margin>+</margin> false. And as we said before, visions appear even to <gloss>those closing / their eyes</gloss>. Moreover, imagination will not be one of those faculties that is always correct, such as <term>scientific knowledge</term> <note>original: "epistēmē"</note> or <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "nous"</note>; for imagination can also be false. 

It remains, then, to see if it is <term>opinion</term> <note>original: "doxa"</note>. For opinion can be both true and false. But opinion is followed by <term>conviction</term> <note>original: "pistis"; a state of being persuaded or having faith in a proposition</note>; for it is not possible for one who holds an opinion not to believe what seems to him to be the case. However, while no animal possesses conviction, many possess imagination. Furthermore, every opinion is followed by conviction, and conviction by having been persuaded, and persuasion by <term>reason</term> <note>original: "logos"</note>; but while some animals have imagination, they do not have-

<summary>Aristotle distinguishes imagination from perception and belief, noting that while perception is always true and present in all animals, imagination is often false and absent in simpler creatures like insects. He further argues that imagination cannot be "opinion" because opinion requires reason and conviction, which animals lack.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, De Anima, imagination, phantasia, sensory perception, opinion, belief, animal intelligence, Greek philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Aristotle’s *De Anima* (On the Soul), specifically entering Book III, Chapter 8. <margin>
Some people seek after and talk nonsense, not according to what he [Aristotle] said; for if someone intends to speak of the soul as something separated <note>Independent of the body</note>, he then leads us away from it being without form <note>The soul requires "form" or structure to function</note>, not according to its existence. <meta>This page continues the analysis of the soul's locomotive power, specifically focusing on how "imagination" and "deliberation" lead to action. It transitions from the physical mechanics of movement (discussed on the previous page) to the cognitive processes—reasoning and desire—that trigger those movements.</meta>

<margin>Sensory <note>original: "ἡ αἰσθητική" (hē aisthētikē); referring here to the sensory form of imagination found in animals.</note></margin>
**Imagination**, as has been stated, is also present in irrational animals. But **deliberative imagination** <note>The ability to weigh different mental images to make a choice.</note> is found only in those with the power of reasoning. For the decision of whether to do "this" or "that" is already a task for reasoning; and it is necessary to measure by a single standard, for one pursues that which is greater. Consequently, the mind is able to create a single image out of several images. And this is the reason why animals are thought not to have "opinion," because they do not possess the type of opinion that comes from a **syllogism** <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note>, whereas the latter [deliberative imagination] possesses it. <insert>...either to possess the opinion resulting from a syllogism or to possess the imagination of the preceding things</insert> Therefore, **desire** does not possess the deliberative faculty. However, desire sometimes overcomes and moves the **will**; <insert>and at other times the will moves</insert> the desire, just as one **sphere** <note>original: "σφαῖρα" (sphaira); Aristotle uses the image of celestial spheres where one moves another to describe how different parts of the soul can push against each other.</note> moves another, whenever **incontinence** <term>akrasia: a lack of self-control where one acts against their better judgment</term> occurs. But by nature, the higher part is always more authoritative and initiates movement. Thus, the soul is moved in three distinct ways. But the **scientific faculty** <note>The part of the mind dealing with unchanging truths.</note> does not move, but remains at rest. Since there are two kinds of judgment—the **universal** premise and the **particular** premise—the first says that "such a person ought to do such a thing," while the second says "this is a thing of such a kind, and I am such a person." It is this latter **opinion** that triggers movement, not the universal one. Or perhaps both do, but the universal remains more at rest while the particular does not.

<meta>This page continues the investigation of the soul's faculties. Furthermore, everything that lives must have a soul from the moment of its birth until its destruction. For it is necessary for a living being <note>original: "ἔμψυχον" (empsychon); literally "ensouled," referring to anything with a spark of life.</note> to experience growth, a peak of maturity, and decay. These processes are impossible without nourishment; therefore, it is necessary for the **nutritive power** <term>threptikon: the most basic faculty of the soul, responsible for growth, maintenance, and reproduction.</term> to be present in all things that grow and decay.

However, **sensation** <note>original: "αἴσθησις" (aisthēsis); including touch, sight, etc.</note> is not necessarily present in all living things. <margin>60</margin> For it is not possible for those whose body consists of a single element to possess sensation, nor is it possible to be an "animal" without this faculty. Nor [can an animal be] anything that is not receptive to the "forms" of things without their matter. <note>Aristotle famously describes sensing as being like wax receiving the imprint of a signet ring without taking the gold of the ring itself—the mind takes the "quality" of an object without the "stuff."</note>

But an animal must necessarily have sensation, unless nature acts in vain. For everything in nature exists for a purpose, or else it will be a byproduct of those things that exist for a purpose. If, therefore, any body capable of movement did not have sensation, it would perish and would not reach its natural end, which is the work of nature. For how will it be nourished? <margin>61</margin> Stationary beings <note>such as plants</note> find their nourishment in the place where they naturally grow; but it is not possible for a body to have a soul and a discerning mind <gloss>to that which is not remaining stationary</gloss> and yet not have sensation, if it is not a stationary being. This applies to generated beings <note>beings that are born and die.</note>; and certainly not to the ungenerated. For why should it not have sensation? It would be better either for the soul or for the body; but now...

<summary>Aristotle argues that while all living things require a nutritive soul to grow, only animals—especially those capable of movement—require sensation to survive and fulfill nature's purposeful design.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, soul, nutrition, sensation, movement, teleology, biology, nature's purpose</keywords>

<margin>§ 11</margin> For if it were simple, it would not have the sense of touch. For the other senses perceive through external media—such as smell, sight, and hearing; but if a creature has no sensation when it comes into direct contact with objects, it will not be able to avoid some things and seize others. If this were the case, it would be impossible for the living being to survive. This is also why **taste** is a kind of **touch**. For taste is concerned with nourishment; 

<margin>§ 12</margin> and nourishment is a tangible body. On the other hand, sounds, colors, and smells do not provide nourishment, nor do they produce growth or decay. Consequently, it is necessary that taste is also a form of touch, because it is the sensation of that which is both tangible and nutritive. This... <note>original: "αὗ-" (au-); a catchword for the next page, likely beginning "αὕτη" (this sense).</note>

<summary>Aristotle argues that touch is the most fundamental sense, essential for any animal's survival because it allows them to identify nourishment and avoid physical harm through direct contact.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Aristotle’s *De Anima* (Book 3, Chapter 12). On the previous page, Aristotle argued that touch is the most fundamental sense required for any animal to survive. Here, he distinguishes between senses necessary for basic existence and those required for "well-being," specifically for animals that move through space.</meta>

-> + <-

It is clear, then, which senses are necessary for the living being <note>original: "ζῷον" (zōon); referring to any creature with a soul and sensation</note>, and it is evident that it is impossible for a living being to exist without **touch**. 

The other senses, however, exist for the sake of **well-being** <note>referring to flourishing or living well, rather than just surviving</note>. These do not belong to just any kind of animal, but only to certain ones. For instance, they must necessarily belong to the **mobile animal** <note>animals capable of moving from place to place</note>. If such a creature is to survive, it must perceive not only by touching objects but also from a distance. 

<margin>65</margin> This distance-perception is possible because the **medium** <note>the material through which a sense travels, like air or water</note> is capable of being affected by the object of sensation, and the animal is then affected by that medium. For just as an object that causes motion in space <note>locomotion</note> produces change until it reaches a certain point, and that which was pushed causes another to push in turn so that the movement travels through an intermediate space—where the first mover pushes without being pushed itself, and the last thing is only pushed without pushing another, while the intermediate does both (and there may be many intermediates)—so it is also with **alteration** <note>qualitative change, such as the way a color or sound moves through the air</note>. 

However, in this case, the alteration occurs while the medium remains in place <gloss>or while it is staying</gloss> and acts by <gloss>or like moves toward like</gloss> being altered <gloss>in this way</gloss>. For example, if someone were to dip an object into wax, the wax is moved only as far as the object was dipped. A stone is not moved at all in this way, but water transmits the motion much further, and **air** is moved to the greatest extent of all. Air both acts and is acted upon, provided it remains still and remains a single continuous mass. This is why, concerning reflection— <note>The text breaks off mid-word: "ἀνάκλασις" (anaklasis), likely referring to the reflection of light or sound.</note>

<summary>Aristotle explains that while touch is necessary for all life, distal senses like sight and hearing are essential for mobile animals to navigate and survive. He uses the physics of "media" (air and water) to explain how sensations travel from a distance.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, sensation, medium, touch, locomotion, alteration, physics of perception, De Anima</keywords>

<margin>64</margin>
It is just as if the impression made in wax were transmitted all the way through to the very end. 

It is clear, then, that it is not possible for the body of a living creature to be simple—by which I mean, for example, made solely of one element like fire or air. For without **touch**, it is not possible to have any other sense. Every living body <note>original: "ἔμψυχον" (empsychon); literally "en-souled" or "animate"</note> is capable of touch, as has been said previously. 

The other senses, besides touch, operate through sense organs, but they all produce perception by perceiving through something else—that is, through **intermediates** <note>the material through which a sense travels, like air for sound or water for smell</note>. For touch consists in being in contact with the object itself. That is why it has this name <note>The Greek word for touch, "haphē" (ἁφή), is derived from "hapto" (ἅπτω), meaning to fasten or touch directly</note>. And yet, the other sense organs also perceive by a kind of touch, but they do so through an intermediary. This sense alone [touch] seems to act through itself. 

Consequently, the body of the living creature could not be composed purely of such elements [like fire or air], nor indeed could it be purely earthy. For touch is present everywhere, acting through tangible things like a mediator <note>original: "μεσίτης" (mesitēs); an intermediary or middle-man</note>. And the sense organ is receptive not only to the qualities themselves as they are, but also...

<summary>Aristotle explains that while other senses require a medium like air to transmit information (comparing it to a mark moving through wax), touch is the most direct and essential sense for a living being, requiring the body to be a complex mix of elements.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the conclusion of Aristotle’s *De Anima* (On the Soul), transitioning into a scholarly commentary or introductory reflection on how different disciplines study the soul. It picks up the thread of how various thinkers—physicians, mathematicians, and logicians—approach the soul's relationship to the body and its eternal nature.</meta>

...they brought forward demonstrations. On the one hand, they considered the soul in isolation, focusing more on the act of **thinking** <note>original: "πρὸς νοεῖν" (pros noein); referring to the intellect or the mind's eye</note>—either as the soul itself or as an object of thought—and how it behaves when it makes use of a body to gain knowledge. On the other hand, there are those who have attempted to speak about the soul from a **physical** <term>physikos: "naturally" or "scientifically," pertaining to the study of the physical world (physics)</term> perspective. These thinkers examine how the soul is ordered in relation to **matter** <note>original: "ὕλη" (hylē); the physical substance of the world</note> and the extent to which it shares a common life with the body. These are the individuals who have set out to speak about the nature of the entire universe. 

Just as they reach conclusions on various other matters, they have approached this subject simply and as a side issue. They explore how the soul is a whole and yet possesses parts; how that same soul enters into communion with matter; and to what extent it possesses a great variety of activities and powers—a nature that is both manifold and diverse. 

And yet, concerning what was left out, they have omitted certain things. Nevertheless, both groups deserve their own particular credit: both the mathematicians and those who seek knowledge, as well as the **natural philosophers** <note>i.e., the "physicists" of the ancient world</note> who examine the soul's nature. Whatever a person cannot grasp on their own, they will find among these thinkers. For instance, the **logicians** and mathematicians explain how the soul is surely **immortal** <note>original: "ἀϑάνατος" (athanatos); undying</note> and indestructible. However, one might better learn about the soul’s relationship to the sensitive faculty and **perception** <term>aisthēsis: the ability to receive and process sensory information</term> from the natural philosophers...

<summary>This page discusses the different methodological approaches to studying the soul, contrasting the abstract proofs of mathematicians and logicians with the physical observations of natural philosophers. It notes that while the former prove the soul's immortality, the latter are better suited to explaining how the soul interacts with the body and senses.</summary>

<note>
**Vocabulary Guide:**
*   **Pascha:** Easter, the central feast of the Christian calendar.
*   **Sunday:** The first day of the week (Kyriake), dedicated to the Resurrection.
*   **Tone:** The Byzantine musical system uses eight "Tones" (Echoi) that rotate weekly.
*   **Menologion:** A liturgical calendar or service book organized by month.
*   **Thomas, Myrrh-bearers, etc.:** Specific themes for the Sundays following Easter.
*   **Pentecost:** The 50th day after Easter, celebrating the descent of the Holy Spirit.
*   **Birth of Christ:** Christmas (December 25).
*   **The Lights:** Epiphany or Theophany (January 6), commemorating the baptism of Jesus.
</note>

<term>Octoechos</term> (Eight Tones): The system of eight musical modes used in Byzantine chant. Each week, the church rotates through these tones, starting with Tone 1.

<term>Paschal Cycle</term>: The period of several weeks before and after Easter (Pascha) where the dates of services change every year depending on when Easter falls.

# The Pascha of Christ <note>original: "χριστοῦ πασχα". This refers to the calculation of the entire liturgical year centered around Christ’s Resurrection.</note>

->6 [Cycles]<- <note>original: "απει ς". Likely an abbreviation referring to a specific chronological cycle or distance within the 532-year Paschal cycle.</note>

---

| | | | | |

## † Preface †

Of the means that provide the goal of prediction through astronomy, O Syrus <note>The dedicatee of Ptolemy’s major works, including the Almagest and the Tetrabiblos.</note>, there are two that are the most significant and principal. One is the study of the order of the powers and the configurations that arise from them overall.

<summary>This page serves as the table of contents and the opening preface for Book I of Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos, listing the foundational concepts of ancient astrology such as planetary powers, zodiacal signs, and aspects. It marks the beginning of the author's formal defense and explanation of how the movements of the heavens affect life on Earth.</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos, Astrology, Planetary powers, Zodiac signs, Syrus, Preface, Ancient Greek Science</keywords>

<meta>Continuity Note: This page marks the formal beginning of Book I of Ptolemy’s "Tetrabiblos" following the table of contents. The author is transitioning from the mathematical study of the stars (astronomy) to the study of their physical effects on the terrestrial world (astrology/physics).</meta>

Of the movements, one [concerning] the moon <gloss>at</gloss> every evening and by almost all is grasped. Secondly, [there is the method] by which, through the **natural movement** of the bodies themselves, we consider certain specific changes produced in the things they encompass; this is a contemplation desirable in its own right <note>original: "αἱρετὴν θεωρίαν". Ptolemy argues that studying the stars' effects is a worthy pursuit of knowledge for its own sake, not just for practical use.</note>. It shares in the connection of the two [methods], concluding in its own arrangement, especially in the demonstration and [within] your own cycle. Concerning the second [method] and this very art, we shall in the present [work] provide an account, as it is fitting for **philosophy**.

Since we have used [these] as introductory sections, let not the weight of attention and unhindered [focus] bypass the nature of what is happening. The weakness found in many [is] because the [study] of the **imitative creation** <note>This likely refers to the difficulty of perfectly "mimicking" or predicting nature's complexity.</note> is joined together; let there be no one who, in the realm of possibility, would <unclear>refuse</unclear> to keep their distance. This is indeed the most reasonable [explanation] for occurrences—clearly [seeking] not from the surroundings, but <unclear>searching</unclear> within oneself. Among those who labor at such things, this [study] has a nature easily slandered by the many. But because the things reported in the **summaries** are entirely the cause of the ignorance regarding changes. For the appearances of the second cause, both toward the starting points and the following of opposites through the beginning, provide the opinions. We shall attempt to find that the [order] of things happening is preserved equally, [speaking] briefly about the **nature of parts**. We exhort you to receive with goodwill the usefulness of such a contemplation as we examine it.

<meta>Continuity Note: This page follows the introduction to Book I of Ptolemy’s "Tetrabiblos." The author has just argued that astrology is a legitimate branch of physical science, transitioning now into a detailed explanation of how celestial bodies physically influence the Earth's environment.</meta>

### The Influence of the Ambient Environment

And it is of an eternal nature that the generation of the **elements** <note>original: "στοιχείων" (stoicheiōn). In ancient science, these are Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> is always changing according to the qualities of fire and air, leading to a diffusion of the **ambient** <note>original: "περιέχοντος" (periechontos). This refers to the atmosphere or the "surrounding" heavens that encompass the Earth.</note>. This environment is itself encompassed by the vapors rising from the earth and the movements within it; it also encompasses the flow of rivers, the waters, and the living creatures that grow within them. 

The origin of these physical effects becomes manifest whenever the **Sun** passes through certain critical points <note>original: "ἀκμὰς" (akmas). These peaks refer to the solstices and equinoxes.</note> of the ambient environment and the regions around the earth. This is evident not only through the seasonal changes which govern the birth of animals, the growth of plants, and the ripening of fruits, but also through the interactions of fire and water. From the Sun come these changes, and simultaneously through the daily cycles, he warms and moistens us, or dries us in the cold. These vapors and the resulting conditions follow the Sun's position at its peak, mirroring the celestial configurations.

The **Moon**, being nearest to the Earth, likewise gives forth an emanation. <margin>The Moon's Influence</margin> Most things, whether **animate or inanimate**, share a **sympathy** <note>original: "συμπάθειαν" (sympatheian). A central concept in ancient science suggesting a hidden "connectedness" or resonance between celestial and earthly bodies.</note> with her. They respond to her luminous flows; for instance, the sea coincides in its tides with her rising and setting. Furthermore, the beginnings of plants and animals, and even certain biological parts, flow and change in unison with her, being affected by her cycles.

In addition to these, the passages of the **fixed stars** and the **planets** <note>original: "πλανωμένων" (planōmenōn) – literally the "wanderers."</note> produce many significant signs in the ambient environment. They create conditions that are torrid, windy, or <unclear>temperate</unclear> in nature, affecting both the voices of earthly creatures and the relationships between them. For their configurations relative to one another, when their various influences meet and reach a symmetry, produce many diverse changes in the world. 

These effects are produced through the power of the Sun, with the other stars acting as contributing causes — <unclear>assisting</unclear> or cooperating in the governance of all things. The influence of the **Moon** <note>The text uses the symbol ☾ for the Moon.</note> is the most manifest and continuous, especially during her conjunctions with other bodies.

<summary>Ptolemy explains how the Sun and Moon act as the primary physical drivers of change on Earth, influencing the weather, tides, and biological growth through "sympathy." He also introduces the secondary but significant role of the fixed stars and planets in modifying these environmental conditions.</summary>

<keywords>ambient environment, elements, Sun, Moon, sympathy, tides, planets, fixed stars, astrology, natural philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 668 ---
<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the discussion from Book I, Chapter 2 of the Tetrabiblos, moving from the Sun's general influence on seasons to the specific, observable effects of the Moon and the fixed stars on the Earthly environment and human activities like farming and navigation.</meta>

...at the full moon. The influence of the stars <gloss>x</gloss> is more periodic and quite visible, as seen in their phases, or rather their waxing and waning. Since this is the case, it follows that not only are things already formed <note>original: "συγκραθέντα" (synkrathenta). This refers to things that have already achieved their physical mixture or 'temperament.'</note> affected in their disposition by the <gloss>x</gloss> underlying conditions, but also the very **seminal principles** <note>original: "σπερματικῶν ἀρχὰς" (spermatikōn archas). In ancient science, these are the "seeds" or formative forces that dictate how a plant or animal will grow.</note> and their fulfillment are shaped by the quality of the ambient environment. 

Furthermore, those among the farmers and herdsmen <note>original: "νομίων" (nomiōn). Specifically those who manage livestock and pastures.</note> who are most observant are able to predict the quality of their future yields from the winds <gloss>x</gloss> that occur during the transitions and settings of the stars. In general, we see that the most significant signs are signaled by the configurations of the Sun, the <gloss>the</gloss> Moon, and the stars. However, some things are observed not only through physical laws but through long-term observation by those who look closely, as we see in all things that can be known beforehand. 

These effects come from a greater <gloss>some</gloss> power and a higher order than the common understanding of the <gloss>the</gloss> masses. Indeed, even some irrational animals <note>original: "ἀλόγων ζώων" (alogōn zōōn). Creatures that do not possess human reason.</note> can sense the annual changes of the seasons and the winds. For while the Sun is the most <gloss>first</gloss> significant cause of such things, the Moon’s influence is also recognized by those who understand the necessity <gloss>the</gloss> of the tides. Similarly, for those who sail the seas, signs of coming storms and winds occur according to a more periodic cycle governed by the Moon itself and the configurations of the **fixed stars** <note>original: "ἀπλανῶν ἀστέρων" (aplanōn asterōn). Unlike the "planets" or wanderers, these stars remain in fixed positions relative to each other.</note> in relation to the Sun. 

Yet, it often happens that people fail in their predictions because, through a lack of experience, they cannot accurately grasp the correct times and places, nor do they understand the cycles of the fixed stars, which contribute a great deal to the result. What, then, prevents us from seeking an accurate opinion regarding the influence of all the stars...

<summary>Ptolemy argues that celestial bodies influence everything from embryonic development to weather patterns, noting that even animals and sailors use these signs. He acknowledges that failures in prediction are due to human error and lack of data, not the invalidity of the science itself.</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos, moon phases, seminal principles, weather prediction, fixed stars, navigation, ancient biology</keywords>

--- Page 669 ---
<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the argument for the validity of astrology as a physical science, moving from the general influence of celestial bodies to the specific observation of their movements and the potential for human error in their interpretation.</meta>

And from the study of these bodies in motion, we ensure that through no particular error of our own, neither the **place** nor the **time** escapes our notice. Having taken these principles from the history recorded concerning them—just as one would with the very nature of these things—we find that they are subject to this shared influence. However, their powers are active and productive; for instance, in the case of the **Sun** <note>original: ☉</note>, we see that it heats, and in the case of the **Moon** <note>original: ☽</note>, that it moistens, and similarly for the rest of the stars. It is in this way that they perform these actions: through a process that is simultaneously natural and aptly derived from the **mixture** <term>mixture: original "syngkrasis," referring to the specific "temperament" or combination of hot, cold, wet, and dry qualities</term> of their particular qualities.

As is possible in each of the given seasons, one can state the properties of the **ambient environment** <term>ambient environment: original "periechon," literally "that which surrounds us," meaning the atmosphere or the air</term> by using these observed phenomena. For example, one might say that it will be hotter or more moist. It is also possible to discern this for each individual case, or the general quality of the mixture of the air, from that same surrounding environment—such as whether a condition is suitable for the body, or of a certain sort for the soul. The events occurring at various seasons are perceived through these factors; thus, the mixture of the air falls upon us as something proportionate and beneficial, or on the contrary, as something disproportionate and harmful. 

These things can be perceived through the powers of such an understanding and through these laws. However, while these matters are easily apparent in outline, they nonetheless face reproach <note>original: "diabolēn," meaning slander or criticism</note>, and it is impossible for them to avoid it. This criticism arises not from the science itself, but from the **fabrication** <term>fabrication: original "plasmatos," referring to the false claims or inventions of unskilled practitioners</term> of those who do not perform the work accurately, and who are many in number. 

As occurs after the multifaceted study of what has happened, or what is incorrectly called the <unclear>paradox</unclear> of the soul, the fault lies not with the **science** <term>science: original "epistēmēs," meaning a structured body of knowledge</term>, but with the inability of those who handle it. This is something one can find in most other arts: practitioners are trusted chiefly because of the title they hold, yet they deceive others through their own opinions about things that only seem to be true. Thus, they are recognized as "experts" even when they speak of things that offer no benefit at all.

<summary>Ptolemy argues that the physical effects of the Sun and Moon on the environment are observable and predictable, asserting that errors in astrology stem from the incompetence of practitioners rather than flaws in the science itself.</summary>
<keywords>celestial motion, Sun, Moon, temperament, ambient environment, atmospheric mixture, scientific error, practitioners, Tetrabiblos</keywords>

--- Page 670 ---
<meta>Continuity Note: This page follows the introduction to the study of the stars, where the author began justifying astrology as a branch of physical science. The previous section established that celestial bodies like the Sun and Moon have undeniable physical effects on Earthly mixtures and temperaments. This page moves into the defense of the art against its critics and the inherent difficulties in achieving perfect accuracy.</meta>

...it provides a starting point for those who are more investigative among those who practice the art <note>original: "philotechnounton" – those who love or are skilled in a specific craft or art</note> to examine and read. However, this is not right: one should not abolish **philosophy** <term>philosophy: in this context, the word "philosophia" refers to the entire body of scientific and natural knowledge, including what we now call astrology</term> simply because some who lay claim to it appear to be wicked. 

But if an investigator—even one who is most agreeable, strictly analytical, and highly trained—pays attention to these mathematical sciences, it is still possible for him to stumble often. This occurs both because of the nature of the things already mentioned and because of the nature of the matter itself. 

Furthermore, the greatest difficulty lies in the weakness of our scientific understanding. Generally speaking, every **theory** <note>original: "theoria" – a way of seeing or a systematic contemplation</note> concerning the quality of **matter** <term>matter: original "hyle" – the physical substance that makes up the world, which the Greeks believed was inherently unpredictable and subject to change</term> is conjectural for everyone and not absolutely certain. This is especially true when dealing with things composed of many different types of elements. 

Moreover, there is the problem of the ancient configurations of the **planets** <term>planets: original "planomenon," literally "the wanderers," referring to the five known planets plus the Sun and Moon</term>. We apply findings from those ancient positions to modern cases that appear to be in the same state, yet those older observations were recorded by observers as being "contained" in a certain way. It would be a matter of "more or less" similarity. And these configurations do not remain exactly the same through a long period of time; because of the change of everything in the cosmos, a state of absolute precision cannot be entirely established.

Some comic poet might be known for his remarks on good or bad things—perhaps deceitfully, or perhaps not at all—but the whole matter would have been settled in a former time. Because of this, even predictions can sometimes fail, as the underlying examples used as models are not truly similar to the present case. 

Investigation should therefore be restricted to the events that arise from the **ambient environment** <note>original: "periechonton" – the surrounding atmosphere or heavens</note>. Among these, some are handled truly and without any weakness being introduced into their movements. 

But concerning **birth-charting** <term>birth-charting: original "genethlialogia" – the specific study of an individual’s destiny based on the time of their birth</term>, it seems that in the case of each individual's unique temperament <note>original: "synkriseos" – the specific "mixing together" of elements in a person</note>, it is not a small matter to see, nor is it always the same. For things happen according to a cause, stemming from the peculiar character of the things coming together. Even the differences in **seeds** <note>original: "spermaton" – referring to both biological heredity and the "seeds" of potentiality at the moment of origin</note> have the greatest power in determining specific traits.

# 4 That it is also useful

Since it has become clear to us that **foreknowledge** <term>foreknowledge: original "prognosis," the ability to know events before they occur</term> through **astronomy** <term>astronomy: original "astronomia." In the 2nd century, this term covered both the calculation of star positions and the interpretation of their effects on Earth, which we now call astrology</term> is possible, and that it reaches only as far as the events of the perishable world and those things that follow for humans from the same cause—these being the initial capacities of their powers, produced overall for the **soul** <term>soul: original "psyche"</term> and the physical body, and their various conditions over time, both long-lasting and short-lived—so that they might not escape our notice as having a most sovereign nature from within, linked to the movements of the gods. Just as in our bodies there is a certain quantity and a way of living together, so too in the soul do we find the expected dignity and the fortunes arising from the appropriate moments. 

Having summarized these points, it remains to discuss briefly how the study of this foreknowledge is useful. We should consider its power toward some good end, or even the opposite, to understand why we should embrace its utility. First, regarding the virtues of the soul, what could be more pleasing for **happiness** <term>happiness: original "eudaimonia," a state of flourishing or well-being</term> and general satisfaction than this very pursuit? Through it, human and divine matters become visible together <note>Ptolemy argues that studying the stars bridges the gap between the mortal world and the divine order of the universe</note>. 

Furthermore, regarding the body, one would better recognize what is appropriate to it through an understanding of its specific fitness, so as to move toward wealth or glory or other such things. This is a point that any **philosophy** <term>philosophy: original "philosophia," meaning the "love of wisdom" or the systematic study of the world</term> would claim for its followers: that none of these external things are truly within our power to acquire or keep. However, the study of the earth, through this science itself, is not to be condemned. The opportunities for greater benefit are clear to those who investigate. Indeed, those who fail to achieve this understanding seem to be looking at nothing of great importance, but merely at the common saying: that because the hardship of all things is destined, **foreknowledge** is superfluous. This is simply... <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing the argument that foreknowledge allows us to prepare for destiny even if we cannot change it entirely.</note>

**astronomy, foreknowledge, happiness, soul, body, philosophy, useful**

<summary>Ptolemy argues that astrological foreknowledge is beneficial because it helps humans understand their physical and spiritual capacities, bridging the gap between the divine and the mundane. He defends the study against critics who claim that knowing a fixed destiny is pointless, suggesting instead that it aids in achieving well-being and managing one's life.</summary>

...not all things are clearly distinguished, so that <unclear>as</unclear> no one may say that what must necessarily happen is [unavoidable]. For if one expects events with uncontrollable agitation, it will be because we are naturally inclined to react to what we possess. <margin>And</margin> foreknowledge, if it reveals hidden things, prepares the soul—which should treat nothing absent as if it were present—to meet each arriving event with peace and stability of mind. Since it is shown from these things that mortals should not think everything happens in this way, and they should follow [this principle]. Just as from the beginning, from some motion toward the forging <note>original: "elasma," referring to the shaping or hammering of material reality</note>, **fate** <term>fate: original "heimarmene," the ordained or "allotted" path of events</term> is thought <insert>to have</insert> not a straight motion, but one resulting from **necessity** <term>necessity: original "ananke," the unavoidable pressure of cause and effect</term>, with no deviation or advance warning. We can see that the motion of the upper heavenly realm is according to fate and unchangeable, being fulfilled by necessity; but the motion in the **sublunary** <term>sublunary: original "perigeio," literally "around the earth," the realm of change and decay below the moon</term> likeness is according to a natural and changeable fate.

For the secondary causes do not take on qualities by accident or as a mere consequence. From these, it happens that the same things fall upon you through a more general circumstance. For neither by one's own fitness or efforts to find relief—as when someone is caught in a greater and hard-to-guard-against surrounding circumstance such as **conflagrations** <note>original: "sympyroseos," catastrophic fires or "burnings up"</note>, or plagues, or floods—will one escape being destroyed. In such cases, the greater and stronger cause acts through the smaller cause. This occurs by the prevailing natural and personal coincidence. Because of the actions and the "antipathies" of the surrounding environment which are not one's own, and which one is unable to bear, it is clear that regarding both the universal and the particular, among those things which are the causes of the laws of accidents, the <unclear>most</unclear> primary cause is not always that from which everything must necessarily result. The accident happens without fail, not because it was indelible for <unclear>everyone</unclear>, but after some knowledge [of the causes].

<meta>This page continues Ptolemy’s argument from Chapter 3 of the *Tetrabiblos*. Having established that foreknowledge calms the soul, he now uses analogies from medicine and natural philosophy to show that even "fated" events can be mitigated if their natural causes are understood and countered.</meta>

These matters being well-considered, we must also look at how things follow according to the nature of foretelling. Therefore, the intellect—drawing from the powers found in **medical science** <term>medical science: original "iatrikes," referring here to the systematic study of cause, effect, and healing</term>—can see this same principle occurring in all things that have **natural origins** <term>natural origins: original "physikas archas," the primary physical drivers of change</term>. We see this in the natures of stones and animals, as well as in wonders, sufferings, and diseases. 

The same outcome naturally occurs unless some **opposing force** <note>original: "enantion," an opposing or contrary influence that can block a natural result</note> acts against it. This is how we should think about both the fated events in the aforementioned natures and in **medical prognosis** <term>medical prognosis: original "prognosei," the doctor's ability to foresee the course of a disease</term>, while avoiding the errors of those who merely wander through the opinions of divination. 

Just as the **active causes** <term>active causes: original "poietika," the planetary influences that "do" or "make" things happen on Earth</term> occur for the most part, some things remain inescapable because they are inherent in the person’s physical disposition and are predicted with total accuracy. This is similar to how those with medical skill use signs to foresee future sufferings. 

However, many things that seem unthinkable can change through available remedies. One might lose hope when powers shift, but we must say that the "coincidence" of medicine exists specifically for all things, in a greater or lesser degree, according to how the subject matches the chronic accompaniment of the **disease** <note>original: "pathos," meaning a suffering, passion, or medical condition</note>. 

Just as a doctor’s inexperience or poor judgment might lead to the belief that rot or decay is inevitable, a similar error happens in understanding nature. Consider the **magnet** <note>original: "magnetis"</note> and **iron** <note>original: "sidiron"</note>. It is a wonder that the magnet draws the iron to itself. Yet, each of these has its own limit. If one does not diagnose the specific conditions of these properties, they will simply follow the power of their inherent nature. No one should think an ulcer is unavoidable simply because it did not receive the proper course of treatment. Nor does the magnet pull the iron if **garlic** <note>In ancient natural philosophy, it was widely believed that rubbing a magnet with garlic would neutralize its attraction to iron. Ptolemy uses this "natural fact" to prove that fated physical properties can be blocked by other physical substances.</note> has been rubbed upon it. 

These things happen insofar as they are governed by natural **antipathies** <term>antipathies: original "antipatheis," the natural "dislike" or counter-action between two substances</term> and by **fate** <term>fate: original "heimarmene"</term>. For these forces are not beyond our reach. On account of this, it is not the case that things simply happen because they are fated, nor that known things fail to happen; rather, they happen according to their nature unless a remedy is applied.

<summary>Ptolemy argues that astrological fate is not an absolute decree but a natural process similar to a disease, which can be mitigated or "remedied" if the practitioner understands the natural "antipathies" (like garlic neutralizing a magnet).</summary>

Regarding the combined signs from which they infer, they act just as if they were preparing their own **nourishment** <note>original: "trophes"</note> so that it might be **well-balanced** <term>well-balanced: original "eukras," referring to eukrasia, the healthy mixture of the four qualities—hot, cold, wet, dry</term>.

It is not difficult to distinguish this regarding the **mixture** <term>mixture: original "synkraseōs," the blending of physical elements</term> or the gift of individual cases; those who [know] either before winters or heatwaves and regarding each individual’s **unique temperament** <term>unique temperament: original "idiosynkrasia," the specific balance of humors in one person</term>. For it is not possible to know the causes again, nor to have many things to guard against. 

It is clearly evident that regarding universal heat and cold, we can cool ourselves or [prepare] if we are about to be burned; this similar action can work through the movement toward a **well-balanced state** <term>well-balanced state: original "eukrasia"</term> for those who are about to suffer from an increase in heat. For this is done either through [reason] or the effort of the faultless. This is the single aim, even if there is [foreknowledge] of the causes and not just a simple prognosis. This very thing, when applied to those who are ignorant of it, creates a sense of the unbelievable.

### 4. Concerning the Power of the Wandering Stars

The Sun and the Moon are the most productive of all, acting by heating and gently drying. These qualities are especially perceptible to us because of the Sun's size and the clarity of the seasonal changes. Since it is positioned near the zenith of our regions, it affects us more strongly in this way. ☉ But the Moon’s power is primarily in **moistening**, due to its proximity to the Earth and the vapors of moisture that rise toward it. Thus, it affects bodies in this way, softening and **decomposing** <note>original: "διασήπουσα" (diasēpousa) — also implies ripening through the breakdown of matter</note> most things. ☉ The star of **Saturn** has a quality consisting mostly of cooling and gently drying. This is because it is, as it seems, the most distant from both the heat of the Sun and the moist vapors of the Earth. <insert>It happens</insert> that power is attributed to this star and the others based on observations of their **aspects** <note>original: "σχηματισμοῖσ" (schēmatismois) — the geometric relationships between planets</note> and their positions relative to the Sun. For in some positions they act one way, and in others another, appearing to increase or decrease their influence upon the **atmosphere** <gloss>that which surrounds us</gloss>. ☉ The star of **Jupiter** possesses a **temperate** <note>original: "εὐκρατέα" (eukratea) — well-balanced or health-giving</note> productive power.

### + On Masculine and Feminine [Planets] +

Again, regarding the natures of the stars, there are two: the male and the female. Among the aforementioned powers, that of the **Moon** (☽) happens to be the most feminine. For the moist element is more abundant in her; according to which, she is also feminine among the **diurnal** <term>diurnal: belonging to the day; active during daylight hours</term> things, whereas the hot element is more characteristic of the masculine. Reasonably, then, they have handed down to us the **Moon** and the star of **Venus** (♀) as feminine, because of the abundance of the moist element in them. But they handed down the stars of **Saturn** (♄), **Jupiter** (♃), and **Mars** (♂) as masculine. 

Because of its nature, **Mercury** (☿) is common to both genders, according as it is productive of either the dry or the moist essence. They say the stars are **masculine** <note>original: "arrenōpon," having a masculine appearance or character</note> in their **configurations** <term>configurations: original "schēmatismois," the geometric relationships or "aspects" between celestial bodies</term> with the **Sun** (☉); for those which are **morning stars** <note>original: "heōous," stars that rise in the east before the Sun</note> and leading the way are masculine, but those which are evening stars and following are feminine. Furthermore, this is determined in relation to the horizons. In the configurations from the rising <note>the Eastern horizon</note> until the midheaven, or from the setting until the subterranean midheaven—as they are toward the eastern parts—they are masculine. But in the remaining quadrants, as they are toward the western parts, they are feminine. : +

### + On Nocturnal and Diurnal [Planets] +

Similarly, since there are two most manifest intervals of those that create time: these happen to be that of the day, which is more masculine on account of the heat and activity within it; and that of the night, which is more feminine on account of its moisture and rest. Therefore, they have reasonably handed down [the following] as **nocturnal** <term>nocturnal: belonging to the night; active after sunset</term>...

These factors also determine that **Mercury** (☿) is diurnal <term>diurnal: belonging to the day; from the Greek 'hemerinos'</term>, and they also include **Saturn** (♄) in this [diurnal] group. Regarding **Mercury**: it is diurnal in its morning configuration, but nocturnal in its evening configuration. They assigned to each of the **sects** <term>sects: original 'haireseis,' the two traditional groupings of planets into Day and Night teams</term> the two remaining planets of a destructive nature <note>original: "phthartikēs ousias," literally "destructive essence"; referring to the malefics Saturn and Mars</note>. They were not assigned to the same causes of destruction, but rather to their opposites. For when things of a similar nature are added to those of a good temperament, it makes their benefit even greater. But when things that are unlike the destructive planets are set against them, it strips away the strength of their maleficence. 

Therefore, they assigned **Saturn** (♄), which is cooling, to the heat of the day to be cooled down; and the star of **Mars** (♂), which is dry, to the moisture of the night. In this way, each planet is brought into a balanced state <note>original: "symmetros," well-proportioned or balanced</note> by its environment, and becomes part of the **well-tempered** <note>original: "eukraton," a healthy or balanced mixture</note> sect. +
